Part II · Chapter 8

Functions as linguistic expressions, and scope

Draft · not yet read by the author

Run on 2026-10-14 22:25 UTC+01:00 inside the library at commit 93d7a39bd: 13 of 13 blocks kept their promise.

The blocks were run by the runtime of the former host language, version 1.27; Haro does not run the library yet. The engine binaries were built in a checkout of this commit, newest built 2026-10-05 20:27 UTC+01:00; 1 engine change(s) committed after that build are not in them.

In this chapter I read a function's name the way the library reads it: a sentence whose prefixes, suffixes and parameters are a grammar. I walk the forms of a name that run, and I count the five that do not. Then I turn to scope: the same verb, three verdicts, with the frame in the verb and not in a flag set earlier. I say what Haro's design keeps of the forms, what it refuses, and what the court proves. The principle is this: a function's name is a sentence, and its prefixes, suffixes and parameters are a grammar that the library can read.

1. The concept, as the field holds it

In the field, a function's name is a label. It follows a convention, camel case or snake case, and it tells you roughly what the function does; the details are in the signature and the documentation. A name does not carry grammar. The related tools are all about structure. Python and Swift offer the keyword argument, so that a call can say which parameter is which. The fluent interface chains calls so that a line reads like a sentence, and the overload gives one name several signatures.

And when the field wants a function to behave differently in a different context, it changes its meaning by a flag set somewhere else. The flag is a mode, a locale, an environment variable. The function's name does not tell you which frame it will run in.

2. The first principle

A function's name is a sentence, and its prefixes, suffixes and parameters are a grammar that the library can read. The paper that first made the claim says, in the words the study of its roots quotes, that it was achieved "without machine learning or NLP systems". It was done by naming conventions that encode meaning, a parameter order that mirrors speech, flexible forms and intelligent defaults.

3. The Softanza form

Look at a name the way the library looks at it. FindNextSTCS: find next, from a start position, with a case flag. RemoveManyCS: remove, many things, a case flag. Each suffix is small and means one thing, and, in these names, the order of the suffixes is the order of the parameters. Here the first name finds. What does the second leave when it removes every occurrence of three letters, whatever their case? Run it:

Haro
o1 = new stzString("123456789HARO")
? o1.FindNextSTCS("haro", 5, FALSE)
#--> 10
o2 = new stzString("SOOooooFFfffTANNnnnZA")
o2.RemoveManyCS([ "o", "f", "n" ], FALSE)
? o2.Content()
#--> STAZA

ran: printed what this block promises

The article promised SOFTANZA on the second line. The run prints STAZA! The code is right and the article is wrong: a removal that does not care about case removes the capitals too. I print the run.

Does the library only follow this grammar, or does it read it? Its name parser, _StzParseName, is an internal helper that no guard covers; I call it first below, for the raw reading. The public way in is ExplainMethod, which explains a method in those terms:

Haro
? @@( _StzParseName("FindNextSTCS") )
#--> [ "find next", [ "case-sensitive", "from-position", "active" ] ]
? @@( _StzParseName("RemoveManyCS") )
#--> [ "remove", [ "case-sensitive", "plural", "active" ] ]
? StzSelfDocQ("stzString").ExplainMethod("RemoveMany")
#--> RemoveMany -- Remove every occurrence of each given substring (mutating).
#-->   (plural form -- applies the operation to many items at once)
#-->   reads as: remove -- over many values at once

ran: printed what this block promises

It reads it. That is the claim, made mechanical: the grammar is in the code and not only in the article. The printed line reads as: remove -- over many values at once is the parser's reading of RemoveMany. The parser decodes the prefixes and the suffixes, the words "except" and "is not", and the voice: a name that ends in ed is passive.

I will walk the forms now. Chapter 5 showed four of them: the active, the passive, the fluent and the named parameter. Here are the others that run.

Z and ZZ say whether a position comes as a number or as a section. A suffix, and the answer changes shape:

Haro
o1 = new stzString("haro php haro ruby haro")
? @@( o1.FindZ("haro") )
#--> [ 1, 10, 20 ]
? @@( o1.FindZZ("haro") )
#--> [ [ 1, 4 ], [ 10, 13 ], [ 20, 23 ] ]
o2 = new stzString("SOFTANZA")
? @@( o2.FirstHalfZ() )
#--> [ "SOFT", 1 ]
? @@( o2.FirstHalfZZ() )
#--> [ "SOFT", [ 1, 4 ] ]

ran: printed what this block promises

The prefix viz changes the kind of answer: a drawing. The position is shown under the text, and an option can number it:

Haro
o1 = new stzString("fjharoljharodjharog")
? o1.vizFind("haro")
#--> fjharoljharodjharog
#--> --^-----^-----^----
? o1.vizFindXT("haro", [ :Numbered = TRUE ])
#--> fjharoljharodjharog
#--> --^-----^-----^----
#-->   3     9     15

ran: printed what this block promises

The plural extends a verb to many things without a loop, and the exceptional form keeps only what you name. The article's example for the second, RemoveNonLettersExcept, does not exist. The form does, in other names:

Haro
o1 = new stzString("__H~~~AR***O__")
? @@( o1.FindMany([ "~", "*" ]) )
#--> [ 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11 ]
o1.RemoveMany([ "_", "~", "*" ])
? o1.Content()
#--> HARO
o2 = new stzString("--Haro--&__Softanza__")
o2.RemoveAllExcept([ "Haro", "&", "Softanza" ])
? o2.Content()
#--> Haro&Softanza

ran: printed what this block promises

The negative is a word in the name, not a NOT around the call:

Haro
? Q("*").IsNotLetter()
#--> TRUE
o3 = new stzList([ "H", "A", "R", "O" ])
? o3.IsNotAString()
#--> TRUE
? o3.DoesNotContain("♥")
#--> TRUE

ran: printed what this block promises

The deep form answers a path, a list of indices that goes as deep as the data does, and the same family replaces and removes at that depth, with :By as its named seat where chapter 5's Replaced said :With; the deep verbs accept both:

Haro
o1 = new stzList([ "you", "other", [ "other", "you", [ "you" ], "other" ], "other", "you" ])
? @@( o1.DeepFind("you") )
#--> [ [ 1 ], [ 3, 2 ], [ 3, 3, 1 ], [ 5 ] ]
o1.DeepReplace("you", :By = "♥")
? @@( o1.Content() )
#--> [ "♥", "other", [ "other", "♥", [ "♥" ], "other" ], "other", "♥" ]

ran: printed what this block promises

The immutable form, QC, runs the whole chain on a copy. After that chain, what does the original hold?

Haro
o1 = new stzString("haxxrxo")
? o1.RemoveQC("x").UppercaseQ().Spacified()
#--> H A R O
? o1.Content()
#--> haxxrxo

ran: printed what this block promises

The chain printed H A R O, and the original still holds haxxrxo!

The misspelled form is accepted, with a note on what stands behind it. A misspelling of a name works:

Haro
? Q("   Haro ").WithoutSapces()
#--> Haro

ran: printed what this block promises

The article says the library recognises and corrects minor typos, and that the intelligence resides in the library itself. The code shows how the form works: WithoutSapces works because that spelling was written by hand as an alias. Another misspelling, WithoutSpces, fails. So the form is real, and in what I traced it is a list of declared aliases; the correction engine the article describes is not among what I traced. I did not trace every file that mentions correction; one message in the object class only suggests a name, with "Did you mean".

Now the scope half of the chapter. The same fault shows up everywhere in programming: behaviour with an invisible governing frame. I hold this as a view, not a result; what stands behind it here is three instances: the regex verbs, the system and the placement of a deployment. A function does one thing here and another there, and nothing in its name says which frame it is in. The answer, in five moves, is the paradigm I call scope-oriented programming. Four come first. Name the hidden frame. Turn it into a small, closed set of named scopes. Choose the scope at the call site, in the verb, and not in a flag set earlier. And give the library the scope to reason with, a semantic handle and not a comment.

It was born in regular expressions, where the frame is how much of the text a pattern must cover. The same pattern, the same text, three verbs: what does each answer?

Haro
cText = "First: Line1" + nl + "Second: Line2" + nl + "Third: Line3"
o1 = new stzRegex("^Second:.*$")
? o1.Match(cText)
#--> FALSE
? o1.MatchFirst(cText)
#--> FALSE
? o1.MatchLine(cText)
#--> TRUE

ran: printed what this block promises

Match answers FALSE: it asks whether the pattern covers the whole value. MatchFirst answers FALSE too: it asks whether the pattern occurs anywhere, with the line anchors off. MatchLine answers TRUE: it makes ^ and $ bind at each line. The frame is in the verb. There is a word scope too, which supplies the word boundaries so that you do not write them. It rewrites the pattern of its object for good, which is why the second instance is a new object with the same pattern. Does the same pattern answer alike under MatchFirst and under MatchWord?

Haro
o2 = new stzRegex("pre\w+")
? o2.MatchFirst("compress")
#--> TRUE
o3 = new stzRegex("pre\w+")
? o3.MatchWord("compress")
#--> FALSE

ran: printed what this block promises

The same pattern answers TRUE under MatchFirst and FALSE under MatchWord!

The second instance is the system. Feature code is written in a named scope, and the same verb gets a different verdict in each. The scope can make a laptop behave like a device it does not have, or refuse what the target forbids. Here, one solution with a backend on a Linux server and a firmware on a small board. What does each system answer when the same verb, Spawn, is asked of it? Run it:

Haro
oSol = new stzPlatformProfile("my-iot-product")
oSol.DevelopedOn(:Windows)
oSol.WithServer(:backend, :LinuxServer)
oSol.WithApp(:firmware, :ESP32)
oBack = oSol.App(:backend).System()
oFirm = oSol.App(:firmware).System()
? oBack.Spawn("worker")
#--> native
? oFirm.ReadPin(4)
#--> rehearsed
try
	oFirm.Spawn("worker")
catch
	? cCatchError
done
#--> scope 'esp32' (espidf) forbids 'process' -- spawn 'worker'. This target has no such capability.

ran: printed what this block promises

this block touches the system; the output shown was recorded on 2026-10-14 22:24 UTC+01:00

The same verb, Spawn, has two verdicts! The server answers native; the board answers scope 'esp32' (espidf) forbids 'process'. The scope decides, not the operation. And the laptop has no pin to read, so the scope answers rehearsed. This is the fifth move: when a scope's capabilities differ from the host's, the library bridges the difference, in both directions. Two declared systems can be compared as data, with a closed set of capabilities:

Haro
oEsp = DeclareSystem("esp32-firmware")
oEsp.SetOSName(:rtos)
oEsp.SetCapabilityList([ :gpio, :network, :clock, :threads ])
oBox = DeclareSystem("laptop")
oBox.SetOSName(:windows)
oBox.SetCapabilityList([ :filesystem, :process, :network, :clock, :threads ])
? @@( oBox.Forbids(oEsp) )
#--> [ "filesystem", "process" ]
? @@( oBox.Requires(oEsp) )
#--> [ "gpio" ]

ran: printed what this block promises

The run printed [ "filesystem", "process" ] for what the laptop can do that the board cannot, and [ "gpio" ] for what the board needs that the laptop lacks. That is the second instance. The third is deployment: the target is the frame, and the scope decides not to ship what the target already does well; chapter 4 showed the plan. The fourth is concurrency, and it is a plan.

The design is next, with what Haro keeps of these forms and what it refuses.

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

In the Haro design, principle 7 makes forms a grammar that the language owns. It is designed and not built: the forms are declared once, and the compiler would generate and check each family. The passive form may not mutate; a verb with Q returns the object; suffix order is parameter order; a W takes a literal parsed at compile time. The spike judges names only: it does not read bodies and it does not judge suffix order. Its first measure is the library's string class: of its 595 shipped spellings of the verbs find, replace and remove, 584 agree with the declaration and 11 do not. I told in chapter 5 what Haro refused as grammar: the misspelled form, the free order of parameters and per-language method names. Here is what it means for this chapter: five forms do not run.

The future form was trimmed on purpose. The header of the natural-code file dates it 10 July 2026: the global queue of deferred actions left, and its FQ and FFQ wrappers were already gone. The reason is written in the design: natural language demands building the whole computational model before executing, and the engine's token plan now does that. It is a plan of the natural engine and no longer a suffix.

The conditional form changed its mechanism. The narration says it no longer goes through eval() but through a small text language that the engine compiles, and that the old extended form, WXT, is now a deprecated alias of W.

For scope, the design document refuses the floating current. Feature code is never written against an ambient "current system". It names its scope. And for concurrency the document records two refusals before there was any code. One is a method per operation that smears the frame across many verbs, such as DoubleEachConcurrently. The other is a mode set earlier. That mode is the antipattern this paradigm was founded against. It also refuses a scope that no host can perform. Its first guess for concurrency was thread vocabulary, and the language beneath has no threads.

I refused to ship the whole engine to the edge. The placement rule is: ship only what is critical and either unique to Softanza or weak on the target. A target that already excels at something gets nothing shipped.

Now the court, and which guards prove which of these claims.

5. The court

00_regex_narrated proves the verbs Match and MatchFirst: Match anchors, MatchFirst searches, Z hands back positions and does not print them. It asserts nothing for MatchLine and MatchWord: the blocks above show them, and only classic blocks, which are not guards, cover them. 972_narration_viz-finding_a_recurring_substring proves the drawn answer. full_scope_model_narrated proves the system scope, with its three verdicts. system_scope_model_narrated proves the closed set of capabilities; one of its assertions is a timing limit, and section 7 says what one probe showed of it. delivery_narrated proves the placement plan.

Where the field does better comes next.

6. The field, and where it leads

The field leads in convention. A name that is a label is easier to teach and easier to type. The grammar of this chapter has to be learned, and some of its forms are rarely used.

The field leads in the guarantee. Python's keyword arguments are checked at the call, and Swift's labels by the compiler, for every function, from the first day. The forms here are judged by the Haro spike, on names and not on bodies, and by the library's own parser, and only in the names that follow them.

On scope, the field leads in maturity. The closest field practice is the explicit context: the Go habit of passing a context to every call, a locale object that carries a frame. They are older and more widely used. What this paradigm adds is that the frame is one of a small, closed set, chosen in the verb, and the library can reason with it.

Last, the limit, with what is built, what is designed and what is absent.

7. The limit

  • builtfourteen of the twenty-two forms, some with examples other than the article's, and three more in another shape; the library reading a name as a sentence; scope in the regex verbs, in the system and in the placement of a deployment
  • designedthe forms declared once as data and generated, in Haro; the scope paradigm for time, units, memory and style
  • absentfive forms: partial, future, free, default and multilingual; concurrency as a scope: a plan with no code

What is built: fourteen of the twenty-two forms of a name run, some with examples other than the article's, and three more run in another shape. The library reads a name as a sentence. And scope runs in the regex verbs, in the system, and in the placement of a deployment. The article counts twenty-three sections: the twenty-two forms of a name, and "small functions", which are functions and not a form of a name. The book's number is twenty-two, the forms of a name.

What is designed: Haro's forms as data, with generated families; and the scope paradigm for time, units, memory and style, as rows of a table.

What is absent, and the page should say each with what exists beside it:

  • Partial, @Removed, is in the archive only: the call is not defined.
  • Future, BeforeQ, was trimmed on purpose, as I said.
  • Free, the suffix that lets a call give its parameters in any order and any subset: there is no definition of it outside the archive. The library's own parser knows the name FX and not FF. The two narrations that tell it use two names, and the code has neither.
  • Default, dftRange and infRange: not defined; the library's comment calls the informing form not yet built.
  • Multilingual, a method named in French or Arabic: not in the live library. The names exist in the archive. The nearest thing today is the language packs of chapter 11.
  • The three that run in another shape. The exceptional form exists, but the article's example does not. Free order, as the article means it, a number and a string swapped in their positions, works for the first order only: in my probe of 8 October, the swapped call ended the program with a status of one and printed nothing. The free order of named parameters is another thing, and chapter 7 runs it. And the statement form is half in place: the "All" half works, and the "No" half is the next step. The library's own classic test promises true on two of its four "No" lines, and the run prints false on all four.

On the scope side: the regex verbs differ from the table of the scope design document in two places. MatchLine lets a dot cross a line, where the table says it stays within one, and MatchOneSegment, which the table offers for the lazy case, is not defined. The system scope is built, and the design document still calls it designed: the record contradicts itself. The scope design document, version 1.2 of 16 August 2026, is quoted here as the document's text. The record does not say who wrote it, and I do not print it as mine. The system foundation document of 20 July 2026 says the foundation is implemented. In one probe run under load, which the book's data does not keep, 61 of the 62 assertions of its narrated guard passed, and the one assertion that did not hold was a timing limit. I state what the code does: the system scope is built, with that result printed beside it, and the design document's word "designed" is the document's, out of date. And concurrency is a plan of record with no code: the word Concurrently has no definition.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerRead a name as a sentence: its suffixes are its parameters, in order.
The analystA position can come as a number or as a section; a name says which.
The designerThe prefix changes the kind of answer: viz draws it.
The decision-makerA scope is chosen in the verb, so the frame is visible where the call is made, and a review can see it.
The educatorThe library parses a name into its sentence, so a learner can ask it what a method says.
The agentWrite the scope in the verb. A call that names a scope is not moved to another frame by a flag set elsewhere.

9. Exercise

Take one verb from a library you use that behaves differently in two frames: a mode, a locale, a target. Say in one sentence what the hidden frame is. Then write, as you would like it to be, two names for the same act in the two frames, with the frame in the verb. Before you run anything in Softanza, take Match and MatchLine on a text of three lines and write what each prints for a pattern that anchors at the start.

Run it. If your two names differ only by a flag, you have not yet moved the frame into the verb.

I left this one in your hands, on purpose. In section 3 the article promised SOFTANZA from a removal, and the run printed STAZA. Here is that block with one change, the last argument of the call:

Haro
o2 = new stzString("SOOooooFFfffTANNnnnZA")
o2.RemoveManyCS([ "o", "f", "n" ], TRUE)
? o2.Content()

not run: an exercise, written for you to run

Run it. Set what it prints beside what the article promised and beside what the first run printed. Section 3 says why the first run did not give the article's line; I do not print what this one gives. When you have solved it, you will know what the case flag decides in a removal, and whether it alone can keep the article's promise.

Part II · Chapter 9

Patterns of thought: the Softanzuter, Reaxis and the engines

Draft · not yet read by the author

Run on 2026-10-14 22:25 UTC+01:00 inside the library at commit 93d7a39bd: 8 of 8 blocks kept their promise.

The blocks were run by the runtime of the former host language, version 1.27; Haro does not run the library yet. The engine binaries were built in a checkout of this commit, newest built 2026-10-05 20:27 UTC+01:00; 1 engine change(s) committed after that build are not in them.

In this chapter I take the three subjects of the title in turn: the Softanzuter, Reaxis, and the engines, of which the timeline and the grid run here. The Regexuter binds a pattern to code that fires and remembers why; Reaxis is reactive programming with its vocabulary redesigned. I climb the ladder the architecture draws, four rungs, and at the third I run the block that fails to cascade rather than claim a rung that is not built. I say what I refused: regex as a way to read text, the field's words for reactive programming, the four siblings, and the cascade. Everything serves one sentence: a Softanzuter is a computational representation of a thinking machine, based on one or many Regexuters, enabling it to identify and react to patterns of thought.

1. The concept, as the field holds it

The field has three tools for making a program react. Regular expressions recognise a shape in text, and nothing more: they say "this matches", and they stop. Reactive programming, the family of observables, subscribers and schedulers that Rx made popular, lets data flow through a program over time. Its vocabulary comes from plumbing, telephony and publishing: pipes, backpressure, hot and cold sources. And rule engines, the production systems of the field with their forward chaining, fire rules when facts appear, and keep firing while new facts appear; that is general knowledge, and the rule engines of the field are older and more mature than anything in this chapter.

Each tool is separate. A regular expression does not trigger a computation, a reactive stream does not recognise a pattern, and a rule engine does not have a vocabulary that a person would use to say a thought. I hold this as a view, not a result.

The next section gives the one sentence I answer with.

2. The first principle

I gave this paradigm one sentence, and everything below tries to make it mechanical: a Softanzuter is a computational representation of a thinking machine, based on one or many Regexuters, enabling it to identify and react to patterns of thought.

The next section shows how far the library has made it mechanical.

3. The Softanza form

The architecture draws it as a ladder with four rungs, each adding one thing.

The first rung is the pattern. You will see it in chapter 15: a shape in a medium, a string, a list, a number, that can say "this matches, and here is how", and do nothing more. The second rung gives a pattern a reaction: the Regexuter, a reflex arc. You bind a pattern to code, process a text, and the code fires on every match. A Regexuter reacts, and it remembers what it did. Here it redacts the secrets in a sentence. What does the state it keeps say about each one: what it matched, what it computed, where, and which trigger fired?

Haro
rxu() {
	Trigger(:SensitiveData = "(password|secret|key):\s*(\w+)")
	@C(:When = :SensitiveData, :Do = '{ @value = "REDACTED-" + len(@value) }')
	Process("User credentials: password: abc123 secret: def456")
	? @@( Results() )
	#--> [ "REDACTED-16", "REDACTED-14" ]
	? @@( Positions() )
	#--> [ 19, 36 ]
	? State()[1][:matchedvalue]
	#--> password: abc123
	? State()[1][:computedvalue]
	#--> REDACTED-16
	? @@( State()[2][:dependson] )
	#--> [ "sensitivedata" ]
}

ran: printed what this block promises

The state is provenance: every reaction that changes a value keeps its why. The last line, [ "sensitivedata" ], is also an honest limit, and I will come back to it: what the Regexuter records as a dependency is today only its own trigger.

Now the third rung, the one the definition is about. It is many Regexuters, over different media, sharing one state, so that what one faculty writes is a medium another faculty can match over. A thought is a state entry with its provenance, and a settled thought is a state in which nothing more fires. That rung is not built, and the block shows how I know. The second trigger below is written for numbers of three digits or more. The first trigger turns the 7 into 700, which is one. If the machine thought in cascades, would the second fire on the first's result? Run it:

Haro
rxu() {
	Trigger(:Number = "\d+")
	Trigger(:Big = "\d{3,}")
	@C(:When = :Number, :Do = '{ @value = @number(@value) * 100 }')
	@C(:When = :Big, :Do = '{ @value = "BIG" }')
	Process("Found 7 items")
	? @@( Matches() )
	#--> [ "7" ]
	? @@( Results() )
	#--> [ 700 ]
	? @@( Triggers() )
	#--> [ "number" ]
}

ran: printed what this block promises

It did not: the results read [ 700 ], the triggers that fired read [ "number" ]. BIG is nowhere! Every trigger is matched once against the original text, and what one trigger writes is not offered to the others. That is the whole difference between the second rung and the third.

The cascade runs one rung above, at the fourth rung, the AI agent: the thinking machine given a body in a world, and a goal. Its mind is made of skills, each with a condition and an action, which chain. The second skill fires on the fact the first one wrote. Pursue() returns how many skill firings were verified, and goes on until the world stops changing, or for twenty rounds at most. What does it answer when asked again?

Haro
oAgent = new stzPIAgent("cook")
oAgent.MemoryQ().Learn("order", "state", "placed")
s1 = new stzAgentSkill("cook")
s1.SetWhen(func oM { return oM.Fact("order", "state", "placed") })
s1.SetDoes(func oM { oM.Forget("order","state","placed") oM.Learn("order","state","cooking") return 1 })
s2 = new stzAgentSkill("serve")
s2.SetWhen(func oM { return oM.Fact("order", "state", "cooking") })
s2.SetDoes(func oM { oM.Forget("order","state","cooking") oM.Learn("order","state","served") return 1 })
oAgent.AddSkill(s1)
oAgent.AddSkill(s2)
? oAgent.Pursue()
#--> 2
? oAgent.MemoryQ().Fact("order", "state", "served")
#--> TRUE
? oAgent.Pursue()
#--> 0

ran: printed what this block promises

It answers 2, then 0, and between the two the fact served reads TRUE. That is a fixpoint. The guard that proves it labels the scene in its own words: the cascade to fixpoint (Softanzuter at agent level). In chapter 17 you will see an agent of this same class refused at a gate. Here is the other face of it: the agent that chains, because its mind is programmatic.

So the word has three meanings in the record, and the reader deserves to be told which is which. First, in this chapter, "Softanzuter" is the third rung, the thinking machine of the definition: designed, not built. Second, the engine has a module with the same name, which the macroplan presents as the foundation for AI agents. Its slots hold a state and a bounded mailbox, and a message into a full queue is refused, counted and never dropped quietly; the agent of the block above, stzPIAgent, never calls it. Third, the design of a universal engine behind all of it, a medium where any pattern language becomes a computation, is planned.

Reaxis is the second subject of the chapter's title, and it is a different idea. It is reactive programming with a vocabulary redesigned from the ground. A reactive thing is a Container, a Stream and an Rfunction: a function in waiting, which is not a callback. Data flows through a stream in plain words, a transformation, a filter, what to do with what passes. Four prices go in, 80, 90, 100 and 120: which ones come out, and at what value?

Haro
aSeen = []
Rs = new stzReactiveSystem()
Rs {
	oStream = CreateStream("prices")
	oStream {
		Transform(func price { return price * 1.20 })
		Filter(func price { return price >= 100 })
		OnPassed(func item { aSeen + item })
		FeedMany([ 80, 90, 100, 120 ])
	}
	RunLoop()
}
? @@( aSeen )
#--> [ 108, 120, 144 ]

ran: printed what this block promises

aSeen reads [ 108, 120, 144 ]: the 80 became 96 and was dropped by the filter; the 90 became 108 and passed. Three functions are in waiting, and nothing here is called a subscriber; the old word Subscribe survives as an alias of OnPassed.

Reaxis replaced backpressure with overflow, a word you do not need a diagram to understand. And it was audited. A reading of the four strategies the article documented found that three of them lost data and reported none. The default discarded everything past the capacity while the counter read zero. That is fixed, and proved for all four strategies. Here, four items go into a buffer of two. What does the stream say happened?

Haro
oRs = new stzReactiveSystem()
oS = oRs.CreateStream("probe")
oS.SetOverflowStrategy(BUFFER_REJECT_NEWEST, 2)
for i = 1 to 4
	oS.Receive(i)
next
? oS.OverflowStats()[:currentBuffer]
#--> 2
? oS.OverflowStats()[:droppedCount]
#--> 2

ran: printed what this block promises

It says currentBuffer is 2 and droppedCount is 2. The counter that read zero now counts!

And for what the field calls debounce, Reaxis says what it means: wait for the attribute to settle. Three changes in quick succession: how many reactions, once the value has stopped changing for fifty milliseconds?

Haro
nSettled = 0
oRs4 = new stzReactive()
oX = oRs4.ReactiveObject()
oX.WaitForAttributeToSettle("query", 50, func(attr, oldV, newV) { nSettled++ })
oX.SetAttribute("query", "s")
oX.SetAttribute("query", "so")
oX.SetAttribute("query", "sof")
oX { ProcessPendingReactions() }
oRs4.RunLoop()
? nSettled
#--> 1
oRs4.Stop()

ran: printed what this block promises

One reaction. nSettled reads 1.

The chapter's third subject is the engines, the small paradigms the library rethought one by one. Chapter 3 gave you truth and emptiness. Two more, run here. Time is a workspace, not a number. A timeline holds spans and computes the gaps and the overlaps. What does it say of the gap between two phases, and what does it do with a point that would fall into a blocked region?

Haro
oTl = new stzTimeLine("2024-01-01 00:00:00", "2024-12-31 23:59:59")
oTl.AddSpan("PHASE1", "2024-01-01 00:00:00", "2024-02-15 23:59:59")
oTl.AddSpan("PHASE2", "2024-03-01 00:00:00", "2024-04-15 23:59:59")
? len(oTl.Gaps())
#--> 1
? oTl.Gaps()[1][:after]
#--> PHASE1
? oTl.Gaps()[1][:before]
#--> PHASE2
? oTl.HasOverlaps()
#--> FALSE
oTl.AddSpan("PHASE2B", "2024-04-01 00:00:00", "2024-05-15 23:59:59")
? oTl.HasOverlaps()
#--> TRUE
oB = new stzTimeLine("2024-01-01", "2024-12-31")
oB.AddBlockedSpan("MAINTENANCE", "2024-06-15 09:00:00", "2024-06-15 17:00:00")
oB.AddPoint("EVENT1", "2024-06-15 08:00:00")
try
	oB.AddPoint("EVENT2", "2024-06-15 12:00:00")
catch
	? cCatchError
done
#--> Point 'EVENT2' falls within a blocked span or blocked point

ran: printed what this block promises

The gap is named by what it lies between, PHASE1 and PHASE2. The blocked span refused EVENT2! The refusal carries its reason: Point 'EVENT2' falls within a blocked span or blocked point.

And a grid has a cursor that knows where it is: position is column and row, and moving past an edge stays at the edge. Two moves down and three to the right, then three more to the right: where is the cursor?

Haro
o = new stzGrid([ 5, 5 ])
o.MoveDown()
o.MoveDown()
o.MoveRight()
o.MoveRight()
o.MoveRight()
? @@( o.CurrentPosition() )
#--> [ 4, 3 ]
o.MoveRight()
o.MoveRight()
o.MoveRight()
? @@( o.CurrentPosition() )
#--> [ 5, 3 ]

ran: printed what this block promises

At [ 4, 3 ], then at [ 5, 3 ]. Three more moves to the right gained one column, and the cursor stayed at the edge!

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I refused to leave regex as a way to read text. I made it a computational medium. A trigger fires a computation, the computation writes a state when it changes the value, and the state records its why. The Regexuter is a faculty and not a mind, and it holds no goal. I added the goal two rungs above it, at the fourth rung, in the agent, on purpose.

I refused the field's vocabulary for reactive programming. Observables, subscribers, backpressure, hot and cold sources, schedulers: borrowed from plumbing, telephony and publishing, and not from the problem. A function in waiting is an Rfunction. Data flows, and nothing is called a producer or a consumer. Overflow replaces backpressure. Waiting for an attribute to settle replaces debounce. The old spellings still work as aliases: feed, emit, send and receive all call one method, so my change was one of naming and not of removal.

I refused to build the siblings. The article that tells the Regexuter describes four more: an analyser, a genetic one, a linguistic one and a quantic one. In the genetic one patterns evolve against a fitness, in the linguistic one triggers are grammar rules, and in the quantic one a pattern can be in several states at once. The article gives each a sample call, and no class stands behind it. The design later found a purpose for two of them. Answering by example demands pattern induction, the genetic one's ground; several acceptable answers demand superposed candidates, collapsed by rules or by choice, the quantic one's. Chapter 18 tells where that stands. They remain a vision; two have their purpose written.

I refused to claim the cascade. The library's architecture says it itself: the scaffolding anticipates cascading but does not yet re-fire dependent triggers to a fixpoint. I would rather show you the block that fails to cascade than a block that does.

5. The court

The Regexuter and the Listexuter have classic tests, and no narrated guard. The Regexuter's eight classic tests ran without error: the folder's log reads PASS 8 ERR 0. Nothing there checks what they print. Five of the Listexuter's seven fail their own expected output, and two promise nothing. The agent's cascade is proved by piagent_narrated, scene five. Reaxis has many guards. 00_overflow_narrated proves the four overflow strategies and the case that loses nothing; 60_reaxis_on_reactor_narrated proves a one-shot timer, the repeating timer, non-blocking HTTP and the settling attribute on the engine's loop. The timeline has test_timeline_regression, which covers construction, duration, adding points and moving the ends, and not gaps, overlaps or blocked spans. The grid has 00_grid_narrated, and deep operations 01_deeplist_narrated.

The next section sets this record beside the field's.

6. The field, and where it leads

The field's rule engines lead. They are older and more mature than the Regexuter, they chain to a fixpoint, and the algorithms behind them are decades old. What I claim is not a rule engine. It is the condition side: rules that are sentences of the pattern languages, over the two media that have a reacting machine built, text for the Regexuter and lists for the Listexuter. The state keeps, for every firing that changes a value, its why. The library's own architecture calls the Regexuter a nascent forward-chaining rule engine, and I will not call it more.

The field's reactive libraries lead in reach. Rx exists in most mainstream languages, with a large set of operators; that is general knowledge. Reaxis is one library on one event loop. The engine's own module for it is a small table of substring rules: the Container, Stream and Rfunction model lives in the library, on the event loop of the engine.

I will not print the star-rating comparison with the field's tools that the library's article on reactive objects carries. It is undated and unsourced.

The next section says where all of this stops.

7. The limit

  • builtthe Regexuter and the Listexuter, reacting with a state that remembers; Reaxis, reactive programming in plain words, on the engine's event loop; the timeline, the grid and deep operations; the AI agent whose skills cascade to a fixpoint
  • designedthe Softanzuter proper, many faculties sharing one state and cascading until it settles; the universal engine behind it; its four siblings, analyser, genetic, linguistic and quantic
  • absenta dependency chain that links one trigger to another; a section-merging verb the article presents as its point

What is built: the Regexuter and the Listexuter; Reaxis on the engine's event loop; the timeline, the grid and deep operations; the AI agent whose skills chain.

What is designed: the third rung, many faculties on one shared state, cascading until it settles. The universal engine for it is planned. The four siblings are vision. The macroplan marks the engine module as done, and the architecture table marks it planned: the same name for two things. That table marks every module of its fifth layer planned, including ones that have source, so it is stale on this point. The universal medium is planned in the engine design document.

What is absent or broken at this commit:

  • The dependency chain is not one. Each state entry depends only on its own trigger, so the chain records which trigger was active and never a link between two. Asking for the chain overflows the stack: the run ends with Error (R4) : Stack Overflow. No test calls it.
  • Five of the Listexuter's seven classic tests fail their own expected output, and two promise nothing. The error log of that folder records, in the sixth file, Error (C8) : Parentheses ')' is missing.
  • A nested list that matches as a whole is reported twice.
  • The article's repeating timer takes three arguments and the library takes two; the form with units is RunEveryXT.
  • Two of the deep-lists article's path verbs, ItemAtPath and ItemsAtPaths, live on a subclass, stzDeepList, and not on a plain list; Paths() is on a plain list.
  • The section-merging article presents a comprehensive verb as its point, and that verb does not exist. The two that do exist, merging what overlaps and merging what is included, run. Section merging has no test file of its own.
  • There is no native engine module for the Container, Stream and Rfunction model: it runs in the library, and the engine's own reactive module is a small table of substring rules. The timeline's guard checks no gap, no overlap and no blocked span; in the classic timeline files, seven fail their expected output and eighteen promise nothing. The grid's engine-backed navigator, stzGridNav, has no test.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerBind a pattern to code, and process; or declare a stream and say in words what happens to the data that flows through it.
The analystTime is a workspace: gaps, overlaps and blocked regions are computed, and a point that would fall in a blocked region is refused with the reason.
The designerThe state of a reaction that changes a value keeps its why: the match, the computed value, the position, the trigger.
The decision-makerOverflow is a number you can read: kept, dropped. A strategy that lost data and said nothing was found by an audit, and fixed.
The educatorThe ladder is a curriculum: a pattern, a reaction, a state, a goal.
The agentYour mind can be skills that chain on what they perceive, until the world stops changing.

9. Exercise

Write a Regexuter with two triggers, one for numbers and one for numbers of three digits or more, with code that turns a number into its triple. Before you run it, write under each question what you expect: what the matches are, what the results are, and whether the second trigger fires on the first one's result. Run it. If the second trigger fires, you have found something I did not.

Then say in one sentence what would have to change in the machine for it to fire, and which rung of the ladder that change belongs to.

I left this one in your hands. Take the second block of section 3 and write its two Trigger lines in the other order, the three-digit one first:

Haro
rxu() {
	Trigger(:Big = "\d{3,}")
	Trigger(:Number = "\d+")
	@C(:When = :Number, :Do = '{ @value = @number(@value) * 100 }')
	@C(:When = :Big, :Do = '{ @value = "BIG" }')
	Process("Found 7 items")
	? @@( Matches() )
	? @@( Results() )
	? @@( Triggers() )
}

not run: an exercise, written for you to run

Before you run it, write down whether the order changes what Results() and Triggers() hold. I do not print the output of this version, and I do not tell you the answer: section 3 says what each trigger is matched against, and section 4 says what I refused to claim. When you can say why, you will know what separates the second rung from the third.

Chapter 10 turns from the machine that thinks to the code that changes. Its title is Programming becomes refinement, and it holds to one principle: stop trying to govern the intelligence, and govern the change.

Part II · Chapter 10

Programming becomes refinement

Draft · not yet read by the author

Run on 2026-10-14 22:25 UTC+01:00 inside the library at commit 93d7a39bd: 9 of 9 blocks kept their promise.

The blocks were run by the runtime of the former host language, version 1.27; Haro does not run the library yet. The engine binaries were built in a checkout of this commit, newest built 2026-10-05 20:27 UTC+01:00; 1 engine change(s) committed after that build are not in them.

In this chapter I say what I mean by refining rather than programming. It is a change to code declared to be changeable, proposed in a typed form, judged by a gate, recorded as a step, and reversible. I run the library's form of it: the refinement point, the proposal, the gate, the cascade, the trust floor and the reversal. And I print the gate as it is, five checks and not the four of my design. I say where the field leads and where the gate stops. The principle is the sentence I wrote on the back cover of my earlier book, Refinement-Oriented Programming: stop trying to govern the intelligence, and govern the change.

1. The concept, as the field holds it

The field has a name for changing infrastructure with a rehearsal: plan, then apply. A tool computes what would change, shows it, and applies it only when you say so. Terraform made the pattern familiar, and the field's admission controllers apply the same idea to a request before a cluster accepts it. More recently, the field has a name for a way of working with code-writing AI agents: specifications first, and the agent fills in. All of this is general knowledge, not a study of the record.

What these share is where they stand. The plan and the admission control are about infrastructure and requests. For the code itself, much of the field's answer to a change is still a diff, a patch of text, and a person's review of it. That worked while every change had a person behind it who could be asked. It is a weak instrument when most changes arrive from agents, in volume; I hold this as a view, not a result.

Against that weak instrument I set one sentence.

2. The first principle

I wrote the sentence on the back cover of my earlier book, Refinement-Oriented Programming, and I have not found a better one: stop trying to govern the intelligence, and govern the change. The library's header says the same thing in the form of a type: a change is a typed proposal, not a diff.

The rest of the chapter runs that sentence.

3. The Softanza form

The practice has changed names in my life. I used to say I programmed. I now say that, more and more, I refine, and I mean something exact by it. A refinement is a change to code that was declared to be changeable, proposed in a typed form, judged by a gate, recorded as a step, and reversible. My earlier book, Refinement-Oriented Programming, tells the discipline through the story of a bank facing a regulator's letter. This chapter tells what the library carries of it.

It begins by declaring where the code may change. A refinement point is a named knob written in the source as a tag, with its kind, its value and its bounds:

Haro
cSrc = 'vat_rate = <R:PARAM name="vat" value="0.20" min="0" max="0.25">' + nl +
       'sort_by  = <R:ALGO name="sort" value="quick" options="quick|merge|heap">'
o = new stzRefinableCode(cSrc)
? o.NumberOfPoints()
#--> 2
? @@( o.RefinementPoints() )
#--> [ [ "vat", "param", "0.20" ], [ "sort", "algo", "quick" ] ]
? o.KindOf("vat")
#--> param

ran: printed what this block promises

A change is then a proposal. It names a point and a value; if it clears the gate it takes effect and is recorded as one step:

Haro
r = o.Refine("vat").To("0.22")
? r[:admitted]
#--> 1
? o.ValueOf("vat")
#--> 0.22
? o.NumberOfSteps()
#--> 1

ran: printed what this block promises

The admission prints as 1 and 0, not TRUE and FALSE: that is how this verb answers, and I print the run. And what does a proposal that does not clear the gate change, and what does the gate say? Run it:

Haro
r2 = o.Refine("vat").To("0.99")
? r2[:admitted]
#--> 0
? r2[:why]
#--> constraint: 0.99 above max 0.25
? o.ValueOf("vat")
#--> 0.22
? o.Refine("sort").To("bubble")[:why]
#--> constraint: 'bubble' not in options quick|merge|heap
? o.Refine("ghost").To("1")[:why]
#--> structural: no refinement point 'ghost'
? o.NumberOfSteps()
#--> 1

ran: printed what this block promises

Three refusals, and the timeline did not grow by a step! The library's comment calls this a law of its own: a rejected proposal never ends changed. Each refusal names its stage first, constraint twice and structural once, as in structural: no refinement point 'ghost', so that a person, or an agent, can correct the proposal without reading a diff.

The cascade is what you read instead of the diff. Before the change, ask what it reaches. There are two cascades, and they are separate. For a point, it is the line it sits on and the other points on that same line:

Haro
cPrice = 'price = <R:PARAM name="vat" value="0.20" min="0" max="0.30"> * <R:PARAM name="margin" value="1.1" min="1" max="2">' + nl +
         'floor = <R:PARAM name="floor" value="0.10" min="0" max="0.30">'
oc = new stzRefinableCode(cPrice)
aC = oc.Cascade("vat")
? aC[:lines][1]
#--> 1
? @@( aC[:alsoTouches] )
#--> [ "margin" ]
? oc.Cascade("floor")[:lines][1]
#--> 2
? len(oc.Cascade("floor")[:alsoTouches])
#--> 0

ran: printed what this block promises

vat sits on line 1 and also touches [ "margin" ]; floor sits on line 2, alone.

For a class, the cascade is a property of the structure of the code: who descends from it and who inherits a method. The library computes it from the code graph, and it can scan a text without touching a file:

Haro
cCls = 'class Tariff' + nl +
       '	def Rate()' + nl +
       '		return 0.20' + nl +
       'class Invoice from Tariff' + nl +
       '	def Total()' + nl +
       '		return 1' + nl +
       'class Receipt from Invoice' + nl +
       '	def Print()' + nl +
       '		return 1' + nl +
       'class Quote from Tariff' + nl +
       '	def Rate()' + nl +
       '		return 0.18' + nl
g0 = new stzRingCodeGraph("")
g0.ScanSource(cCls, "world.ring")
g0.BuildGraph()
? @@( g0.Cascade("Tariff")[:descendants] )
#--> [ "Invoice", "Quote", "Receipt" ]
? g0.Cascade("Tariff")[:blastRadius]
#--> 3
? @@( g0.ImpactOf("Rate")[:inheritedBy] )
#--> [ "Invoice", "Receipt" ]

ran: printed what this block promises

Change the rate of the tariff and three classes are in the blast radius. Two of them inherit the method, and ImpactOf names them: [ "Invoice", "Receipt" ]. The third, Quote, redefines it, so it owns the method and does not merely inherit it. That is the difference ImpactOf draws.

How does a change reach its dependents? By a rule that spans several points, judged on the state the change would produce. If the rule fails, the value is put back:

Haro
d = new stzRefinableCode(cPrice)
d.DeclareDerivation("vat-above-floor",
	func oCode { return ring_number(oCode.ValueOf("vat")) >= ring_number(oCode.ValueOf("floor")) },
	"vat must not drop below floor")
? d.Refine("vat").To("0.30")[:admitted]
#--> 1
r3 = d.Refine("vat").To("0.05")
? r3[:admitted]
#--> 0
? r3[:why]
#--> derivation: rule 'vat-above-floor' violated -- vat must not drop below floor
? d.ValueOf("vat")
#--> 0.30

ran: printed what this block promises

The rule refused the change and named itself: derivation: rule 'vat-above-floor' violated -- vat must not drop below floor. The value is still 0.30.

And who proposed it? Every proposal carries its origin, and a point can set a floor of trust that refuses a lower origin, without refusing a person. What happens to a proposal from a language model when the floor of the point asks for a trusted origin? Run it:

Haro
d.TrustFloor("vat", :trusted)
r4 = d.Refine("vat").As(:llm).To("0.25")
? r4[:admitted]
#--> 0
? r4[:why]
#--> trust: posture :llm below the required floor for 'vat'
? d.ValueOf("vat")
#--> 0.30
? d.Refine("vat").As(:trusted).To("0.25")[:admitted]
#--> 1
? d.PostureOf(d.NumberOfSteps())
#--> trusted

ran: printed what this block promises

The model's proposal was refused: trust: posture :llm below the required floor for 'vat'. The point kept 0.30! The same proposal from a trusted origin was admitted, and the step records trusted.

And who may turn which knob? That is declared, too: a permission, and an authority level against a risk tier. Take a delegated actor and a knob of the third tier. Run it:

Haro
gv = new stzRefinableCode(cPrice)
gv.SetGovernedBy(new stzGovernance("release-ops")).SetActor("release-bot")
gv.SetRiskFor("vat", 3).SetAllowRefine("vat").SetAuthorityLevel(:Delegated)
r5 = gv.Refine("vat").To("0.22")
? r5[:admitted]
#--> 0
? r5[:why]
#--> governance: refused: 'release-bot' holds 'delegated' authority (level 2) but 'refine-vat' is risk tier 3 (SHOULD does not cover it)
? gv.ValueOf("vat")
#--> 0.20
gv.SetAuthorityLevel(:Autonomous)
? gv.Refine("vat").To("0.22")[:admitted]
#--> 1
? gv.GovernanceQ().NumberOfDecisions()
#--> 1

ran: printed what this block promises

The delegated actor was refused, 'release-bot' holds 'delegated' authority (level 2), and the value stayed 0.20. The same proposal was admitted once the actor was escalated! The decision is recorded: NumberOfDecisions() printed 1.

Last, can a step be taken back? Reversibility is part of the data model: every admitted step keeps its prior value. Rewind to a named checkpoint, rewind to zero, go forward again:

Haro
t = new stzRefinableCode(cPrice)
t.Refine("vat").To("0.21")
t.Refine("vat").To("0.22")
t.Checkpoint("reviewed")
t.Refine("vat").To("0.28")
? t.ValueOf("vat")
#--> 0.28
t.RevertToCheckpoint("reviewed")
? t.ValueOf("vat")
#--> 0.22
? t.NumberOfSteps()
#--> 2
t.RevertTo(0)
? t.ValueOf("vat")
#--> 0.20
? t.CanRevert()
#--> 0
t.Redo()
? t.ValueOf("vat")
#--> 0.21

ran: printed what this block promises

At zero, CanRevert() printed 0. One Redo(), and the value is 0.21, the first step again.

That is the gate in the form the library has it. Five checks, in the order the code runs them. The structure of the proposal, then the constraints of the point, then the governance, then the trust of the origin, and last the derivation across points. I ran them above in the order of the story, not of the code. The header of the file calls this a four-stage gate in one line and five in another. The code numbers its checks 1, 2, 3, 4 and 4b. The trust check was added to the four on 16 July 2026, and the design's count was not changed. I report what runs: five checks.

Behind the gate stand decisions, and what I refused.

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I refused to govern the intelligence. Much of the field's approach to AI agents is to make the model safer: alignment, guardrails, a prompt that asks for confirmation; that too is general knowledge. I refused that frame. A model's output is whatever it is, from whichever model, and the intelligence of the next generation will not hold still for me to govern it. The change is the thing that stays, and it is the thing that reaches the world. So the gate stands where the change arrives, and it asks one thing: what is proposed, from where, and does the code say this point may change that way.

I refused the diff as the unit. A diff is a text change. A refinement is a typed proposal about a declared point, with a kind, bounds and an origin. I kept the diff as an artefact, and I refused it as the thing to review.

I made the library carry the verb, and left the environment elsewhere. The refinement as a library verb, the point, the gate, the cascade and the reversal, belongs to the open foundation. The environment in which a team lives with it day to day, the screens, the live mode, the book, is a product. It does not leak into the library.

I printed the gate as it is. I wrote the design with four stages, and the code has five checks. A page that quotes my design and not my code would be wrong, and it is the code that runs.

5. The court

refinablecode_narrated proves the point declared, the proposal that passes, the two refusals that leave the source whole (bounds and options), the cascade, the reversal, and the saved file. refine_deepening_narrated proves the timeline with its checkpoints and its redo, and the trust floor. gate_deepening_narrated proves the refusal of an unknown point, the derivation across points with its rollback, and the governed refusal with its lineage.

Next comes the field, and where it leads.

Read from the library's test tree at commit 93d7a39bd on 2026-10-14 22:28 UTC+01:00. The figure is the number of assertions the guard holds, counted in its file; the site shows each one run.

  • refinablecode_narrated17 assertionsbase/test/refine/refinablecode_narrated.ring
  • refine_deepening_narrated24 assertionsbase/test/refine/refine_deepening_narrated.ring
  • gate_deepening_narrated19 assertionsbase/test/refine/gate_deepening_narrated.ring

6. The field, and where it leads

The field leads in infrastructure, where plan and apply are the daily practice of many teams and the apply talks to real providers; this is general knowledge, as in section 1. Softanza's gate is about the change to code, which the field handles with a review.

The field's tools lead in breadth: they are not tied to one library, one language, or one declared knob. Softanza's gate judges what the code declared as a point. A change to a place that was never declared is not a refinement here; it is outside the gate.

And on trust, much of the field's approach is built to scale to any AI model. Mine rests on one declaration per point.

Now, where the gate stops.

7. The limit

  • builtthe refinement point declared in the source; the gate with five checks; the cascade of a point and of a class; reversal by step, by checkpoint and to zero; the trust floor and governed refining
  • designedthe experience the article describes: asking a point to explain itself, applying a plan, a one-line refinement; the cascade of the code graph joined to the gate; the refinement seat of Haro
  • absenta saved history: the file keeps the source and nothing of the timeline

What is built: the refinement point, the gate with its five checks, the cascade of a point and of a class, the reversal, the trust floor, and governed refining. The guards of section 5 cover them, with two exceptions. The cascade of a class has no guard here, because the code-graph guard scans a live path of the library's working tree. And no guard asserts the other points on a line.

What is designed, and absent from the library by name: the experience the original article describes. The class that article names, stzPolyCode, is not in the library at this commit. The one-line refinement of the design document, a point that explains itself, a plan that is applied, are not in the library. The cascade of the code graph and the cascade of the gate are not joined. And Haro has a gate in a spike written only in the former host language, with its own seat for refinement not built.

What is built, and where it stops: the limits of the gate as it stands.

  • It checks the constraints of three kinds of point, a parameter, an algorithm and a library. A point of another kind, a block of code for instance, parses and passes without a check; checks for those kinds are the next step.
  • An unknown trust posture ranks as trusted: the code gives it the top rank. So a proposal from an origin the code does not know clears a floor of trusted.
  • A derivation is applied tentatively and restored on failure. So I say "never ends changed", not "never touched".
  • The saved file holds the rendered source; the history, the postures, the timeline and the load-back are absent, and are the next step. Reversibility lives in the running object, and carrying it into the file is still to come. The library writes this file with the suffix .zrfn, as shipped. The Haro charter, ratified on 1 October 2026, takes the suffix .rfn for the refinement sentence of Haro, and leaves .zrfn to the library's lift from comment tags, the form this chapter ran.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerDeclare the places that may change, and propose changes to them as typed proposals. A refusal names its stage.
The analystThe rule that spans several points is yours to declare, and the gate judges it on the state the change would produce.
The designerThe cascade is what you read instead of the diff: for a point, which line and which points on it; for a class, which classes inherit. They are two cascades, not yet one.
The decision-makerWho may turn which knob is a permission and an authority against a risk tier, and the decision is recorded with its authority at the time.
The educatorStep back one, rewind to a named checkpoint, rewind to zero, go forward again. A learner can try without fear because every step keeps its prior value.
The agentYou may propose. Your origin is on the proposal, and a point can set a floor your origin does not clear.

9. Exercise

Take two settings of a program of yours: a rate and a ceiling, say, with a rule that the rate must stay below the ceiling. Declare them as points, with bounds, and declare the rule across them. Before you run anything, write under each proposal whether it is admitted and, if not, at which stage it is refused. Propose a change of the rate above the ceiling, and one from an origin you declare as an AI model, against a floor you set. Then rewind to zero and go forward one step.

Run it. If you were wrong about the stage, you have found a place where your own gate disagrees with your own expectation.

I left this one in your hands. Section 7 says what the gate does with an origin the code does not know, and the trust block of section 3 is the block to run. Its first lines are below, and d is the object of that block, so run section 3 first; change one thing, and replace :llm with a name of your own, one the code was never told about.

Haro
d.TrustFloor("vat", :trusted)
r4 = d.Refine("vat").As(:yourorigin).To("0.25")
? r4[:admitted]

not run: an exercise, written for you to run

Run it, and read what the gate does against what section 7 says it does. I will not tell you whether the gate is right. When you have decided, you will know what the trust floor does with an origin it has never met.

The next chapter states a law: a language is declared and closed, and whatever speaks it, a person or a model, is judged by it. Here the thing judged was a change; there it is whoever speaks.

Part III · Chapter 11Spine

Law: a language is declared and closed, and whatever speaks it, person or model, is judged by it

Draft · not yet read by the author

Run on 2026-10-14 22:25 UTC+01:00 inside the library at commit 93d7a39bd: 11 of 11 blocks kept their promise.

The blocks were run by the runtime of the former host language, version 1.27; Haro does not run the library yet. The engine binaries were built in a checkout of this commit, newest built 2026-10-05 20:27 UTC+01:00; 1 engine change(s) committed after that build are not in them.

In this chapter I state the law of Part III and run it. I begin with a sentence that runs because every word of it is in a dictionary the library owns, in English, Hausa, French and Arabic. I show what the library says about a word it does not know. Then I declare the shape of an answer as a schema, judge answers against it, and show the one thing a grammar cannot kill: a false answer in the right shape. I say which guards prove this, where the field is ahead, and where the natural layer is not yet closed, which the law states. The law itself is one sentence: a language is declared and closed, and whatever speaks it, a person or a model, is judged by it.

What the AI age changes here

In Part II, the age changed who writes the code. Here it changes who speaks the sentence. A sentence of a language used to have a person behind it, someone who could be asked what they meant. Today the writer of a sentence can be an AI model, which cannot be asked, and which will write a fluent sentence whether or not it is true.

So the grammar must be closed, and the court, the part that accepts or refuses a sentence by its grammar, must read it. A language whose sentences may contain anything cannot refuse anything, and a court cannot judge a sentence it cannot read. The vision of the platform puts the whole movement in one line, which I ratified: humans and machines meet in declared languages, small, closed and judged, not in general-purpose code.

This is also where the order of the book turns around. The cover goes from the familiar to the new: programming, languages, intelligence. The record's logic goes the other way. The first act is to declare a language. Programming, the discipline of Part II, happens inside declared languages: the forms of the vocabulary are already a declaration in Haro, in a spike, a short experiment written to try a design, outside the library. Intelligence, Part IV, is governed by both: a model is held to a declared grammar before it speaks, and its sentence is judged after. The book keeps the cover's order, so this chapter sits in the middle; in the record's order it would come first.

1. The concept, as the field holds it

For a working programmer, a language is a general host, Python, JavaScript, Java. A "domain language" is usually a library whose calls read like sentences, while the file around them may contain any code of the host. The estate's own study of the field, written in August 2026, names what happened to those designs. Internal languages died of openness, because a build file is declarative only until someone writes arbitrary code in it. Language workbenches died of the weight of their tools. And it names the languages that won: SQL, regular expressions, Make, HTML and CSS, the configuration languages. Its verdict is that they won because they are closed.

The model era added one practice: when an AI model writes, either check what it wrote, or constrain its output while it writes, with a grammar or a schema. The reference implementation of grammar-constrained sampling is an open project, and the record says so where it uses the same algorithm. And in the field's common language today, "programming in natural language" means one thing: prompting a model.

2. The first principle

A language is declared and closed, and whatever speaks it, a person or a model, is judged by it.

3. The Softanza form

Can a sentence run without an AI model guessing what it means? It can, when every word of it is in a dictionary the library owns:

Haro
Naturally("
    Make a string with 'hello niger' inside
    Spacify it and uppercase it
    @Box it while the box@ is rounded
    Display it on the screen
")
#--> ╭───────────────────────╮
#    │ H E L L O   N I G E R │
#    ╰───────────────────────╯

ran: printed what this block promises

Four lines of English became a rounded box around spaced capitals.

The dictionary is data, keyed by meanings, not by English words. So can the same meaning be said in another language by adding a block of data, not code? Here is one instruction in English, in Hausa, in French and in Arabic. The Hausa sentence is the narration's own, and the French one comes from the library's guard with its data changed. I composed the Arabic one from the library's vocabulary. No native speaker has read the Hausa or the Arabic as far as the record shows:

Haro
? Naturally("Create a string with 'hello' and uppercase it").Result()
#--> HELLO
? NaturallyIn("hausa", "Yi rubutu dauke 'hello' Maida shi").Result()
#--> HELLO
? NaturallyIn("fr", "Crée une chaine avec 'hello' et mets la en majuscules").Result()
#--> HELLO
? NaturallyIn("ar", "أنشئ نصا بـ 'hello' ثم كبّره").Result()
#--> HELLO

ran: printed what this block promises

Four languages, one meaning, and HELLO four times.

And a program says back what it understood, in its own language. A person reading Arabic can check the machine's reading of their sentence without reading a line of code.

Haro
o1 = NaturallyIn("ar", "أنشئ قائمة بـ [ 5, 3, 5 ] ثم أزل تكراراتها")
? @@( o1.Result() )
#--> [ 5, 3 ]
? o1.Understood()
#--> أنشئ قائمة بـ [ 5, 3, 5 ] -> أزل التكرارات

ran: printed what this block promises

The program said back أنشئ قائمة بـ [ 5, 3, 5 ] -> أزل التكرارات: the list it was given, and the removal of duplicates.

Now the part the library does by rule: say what it did not understand. What does it do with a verb it does not know? Misspell one and run it:

Haro
o1 = Naturally("Create a string with 'softanza' Uppercse it")
? o1.Result()
#--> softanza
? @@( o1.Unresolved() )
#--> [ [ "Uppercse", "uppercase" ] ]
? o1.UnderstoodAll()
#--> 0

ran: printed what this block promises

The misspelled verb is not guessed. Unresolved() answers [ [ "Uppercse", "uppercase" ] ], the word it met beside the word the library thinks you meant, and UnderstoodAll() answers 0: the program admits that it did not understand everything. That is the permissive mode: an unknown word is skipped and reported. An AI agent gets the strict mode, which refuses, and a world, a declared list of allowed operations, can limit its sentences to that list:

Haro
try
	NaturallyStrict("Create a string with 'x' Fooify it")
catch
	? cCatchError
done
#--> Strict natural mode: not understood: 'Fooify' (did you mean 'boxify'?)
try
	NaturallyStrictIn("en", "Create a list with [ 3, 1 ] Reverse it", [ "METHOD_REMOVEDUPLICATES" ])
catch
	? cCatchError
done
#--> Operation not permitted in this world: METHOD_REVERSE

ran: printed what this block promises

Strict mode refuses 'Fooify' and still names the nearest word: did you mean 'boxify'?. In that world, a sentence that reverses a list is refused! The refusal names the operation: Operation not permitted in this world: METHOD_REVERSE.

The other direction of natural code in Softanza is the near-natural chain, where the person is the parser and the chain reads as a sentence. When it answers no, does it say why?

Haro
? IsQ().TheQ().LengthQ().OfQ("softanza").LessThanQ().TheQ().LengthQ().Of("Haro")
#--> 0
? Why()
#--> no: 8 is not less than 4

ran: printed what this block promises

The chain answered 0, and Why() gave the reason: no: 8 is not less than 4. A verdict says why.

Now the law at its sharpest: an AI model. The library declares the shape of an answer as a schema. What happens to a schema that names a type the library does not have? It is judged when it is declared, before any model is called:

Haro
try
	StzOutputSchemaQ([ [ :field = "x", :type = :colour ] ])
catch
	? cCatchError
done
#--> stzOutputSchema: unknown field type 'colour' (use string|number|boolean|oneof|list|structure).

ran: printed what this block promises

The refusal names the unknown type, 'colour', and lists the six it accepts: (use string|number|boolean|oneof|list|structure). The schema was refused before any model was called! A correct schema is a small closed language. The court judges any answer against it, whoever wrote the answer. And the schema emits its grammar, so that a model can be held to it while it writes:

Haro
oS = StzOutputSchemaQ([
	[ :field = "name", :type = :string ],
	[ :field = "age",  :type = :number, :must = [ [ ">=", 0 ], [ "<=", 130 ] ] ],
	[ :field = "mood", :type = :oneof,  :choices = [ "positive", "negative" ] ]
])
? oS.Accepts("name: Hadiza" + nl + "age: 41" + nl + "mood: positive")
#--> 1
? oS.Accepts("name: Hadiza" + nl + "age: 41" + nl + "mood: angry")
#--> 0
? oS.Accepts("name: Hadiza" + nl + "age: 900000" + nl + "mood: positive")
#--> 0
? oS.Accepts("name: Hadiza" + nl + "age: 62" + nl + "mood: positive")
#--> 1
? oS.ToGBNF()
#--> root ::= name-line age-line mood-line
#    name-line ::= "name: " text "\n"
#    age-line ::= "age: " number "\n"
#    mood-line ::= "mood: " ("positive" | "negative") "\n"
#    text ::= [^\n]+
#    number ::= "-"? [0-9]+ ("." [0-9]+)?
#    boolean ::= ("yes" | "no" | "true" | "false")

ran: printed what this block promises

Look at the four verdicts. The first answer printed 1. The second, with mood: angry, and the third, with age: 900000, printed 0: the court refused both. The fourth printed 1 again. Hadiza is forty-one in the first answer and sixty-two in the fourth, and the court accepts both! A grammar kills malformed sentences, not false ones. The record says it in five words: structure kills malformedness, not falsehood. This book says the same: the truth of an answer is not for the grammar. The record says that truth needs reversibility, an auditor and a Principal, the person who rules. A grammar is the gate, not the judge of everything. The grammar also prints a boolean rule that no field of this schema uses.

A template is a contract too. A sentence with an unfilled hole is refused before it runs:

Haro
try
	NaturallyWith("Create a string with {#1} and {#2} it", [ "x" ])
catch
	? cCatchError
done
#--> Unfilled template hole! The narration still contains a {#n} slot with no value for it.

ran: printed what this block promises

And patterns are small languages of their own, though not yet closed ones: chapter 15 shows the pattern classes accepting a word they do not know, without complaint. The shape of a list is declared, not written as a loop:

Haro
? Lx("[@N, @S]").Match([42, "hello"])
#--> 1
? Lx("[@N, @S]").Match(["hello", 42])
#--> 0
? Lx("[@N, [@N2], @N]").Match([1, [2, 3], 4])
#--> 1
? Lx("[@N, [@N2], @N]").Match([1, [2], 4])
#--> 0

ran: printed what this block promises

Two shapes matched, two did not, and no loop was written.

The chapters of this part prove the law from five sides. Chapter 12 tells a language declared: the forge (the machinery that produces a language's parser, court, printer and grammar from its declaration alone), the closed grammar with no escape into the host, and the court born with the grammar. It tells too the grammar emitted so that a model can only speak valid sentences, and the parts a declaration yields. Chapter 13 tells the two directions of natural code, the machine as the parser and the person as the parser, in one discipline. Chapter 14 tells knowledge programming, one file that is a system. Chapter 15 tells the pattern languages, regex lifted to lists, numbers, tables, matrices, time and graphs. Chapter 16 tells the seven languages Softanza reaches through one governed door, and why a door is not a facet.

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I chose the act: declare a language. Not "use our language". Declare yours: the language of your domain, in your words. That is the kernel of the platform, and it is the reason this part exists.

I refused the open escape. The meta-language that declares languages in the estate lives outside this library. Its founding rule refuses to define any form that would let a sentence reach host code, call a function, evaluate a string or touch a file. Not forbidden: unexpressible. An internal language that cannot refuse arbitrary host code is, in the words of the estate's field study, an API wearing a language's costume.

I refused natural language as a way to declare. Natural language asks; it never declares. A model may draft a declaration, and by the vision's rule, which is designed and not yet built, the draft enters the world only as a proposal: the model proposes, the court decides, a person ratifies.

I kept the promise of 2020 and changed its mechanism. My first slide promised executable natural language. The vision of 2026 judged that slogan: it promised more than a court can defend, because a natural sentence can be ambiguous and a lie can be grammatical. So the naturalness stays at the door, where a sentence asks or drafts, and the execution belongs to closed languages a court can judge. I built the natural layer that way long before the vision named it. Only words defined in the dictionary are interpreted. Every other word is skipped and reported, or refused in strict mode, never guessed.

I took governance out of the library and kept the refusals in it. In July 2026, a kit for governing AI agents landed inside the natural layer. I removed it the same day: the strict mode, the refusals, the why and the understood belong to the library; a product for governing agents does not. And I removed a set of markers, suffixes that marked a reference, which chapter 13 tells: their letter-order cipher had been inverted by its own inventor, from memory, and they duplicated meanings. A language a person speaks never marks a reference that way. An ungrammatical chain that runs is a bug.

I refused a second embedding. Chapter 1 states that decision; here I add only that a door brings a foreign runtime, a facet brings a familiar syntax over the same grammar, and chapter 16 tells the difference.

5. The court

multilingual_pack_narrated proves the languages as data: the packs, the programs in French and Arabic, a pack added at runtime, and the program paraphrasing back in its own language. semantic_resolver_narrated proves the unknown word with its suggestion, the strict mode, and the allow-list under which everything off the list is grammatically impossible. Its run does not yet reach its end at this commit. I ran it twice on 8 October 2026, for chapter 13, and each time it stopped with an error raised from a string-splitting function, before its last assertion. So the page counts its assertions and does not claim its verdict. literate_templates_narrated proves that a template is a contract. question_narrated proves that a yes-or-no verdict records its why. structuredoutput_narrated proves the court of structured output, including the lie it lets through. schema_grammar_narrated proves the grammar compiler, and constrained_decoding_narrated the sampler that holds a model to it.

Seven guards prove the law; the next section says where the field is ahead of it.
