6. The field, and where it leads

The field leads in tools. The language workbenches remain ahead on the axes the estate's design deliberately gave up: projectional tooling (editors that understand a language as you type), IDE integration, macro-theoretic depth. The estate's study says it in its own words: that is a bet, and it is named as one.

The field built constrained decoding first. Softanza's sampler follows the reference implementation's algorithm and vendors nothing. Measured against one small model of a hundred and thirty-five million parameters, on ten prompts, the answers were valid at the first attempt two times in ten when checked afterwards. Held to the grammar, the model was valid ten times in ten. That is one small model and ten prompts, and nothing in the record measures a large one.

And the age cuts both ways. Generated code makes careless language-making cheap too. That is why the court is not an accessory of a declared language. It is the core. This is my view.

7. The limit

  • builtthe natural layer's vocabulary as data in five languages, with its refusals; the court of structured output, its grammar compiler and its sampler; the pattern languages, which accept a word they do not know
  • designedthe forge that produces a language's parser, court and grammar from its declaration alone; a grammar emitted for every declared language; the writing style as a declared grammar
  • absenta natural layer closed all the way down: one form of list still reaches host code; pattern classes that refuse a word they do not know; the standard Hausa letter ɗ in the Hausa pack

What is built: the natural layer, its vocabulary as data in five languages, English, Hausa, French, Arabic and Turkish, and its refusals. Built too: the court of structured output with its grammar compiler and its sampler, and the pattern languages. These accept a word they do not know today; closing them is to come.

What is designed: the forge that would produce, from a language's declaration alone, its parser, its court, its printer (the part that writes a sentence back out) and its grammar for a model. The forge is built outside the library and designed for the library: a first sketch of it was built outside the library in October 2026. The library cannot run it yet. The vision's text says the forge has not yet forged (made a language's parts from its declaration). The sketch has since forged courts and grammars for several languages, judged by those languages' own fixtures, and the vision has not caught up. Chapter 12 tells it with its limits. A grammar for every declared language is designed and to come.

What is absent, and the law states it. The natural layer is not closed all the way down. One form, a list written inside brackets, is still handed to the host to evaluate. Does a host function inside the brackets run? Try one:

Haro
? @@( Naturally("Create a list with [ upper('x'), 1 ] and remove its duplicates").Result() )
#--> [ "X", 1 ]

ran: printed what this block promises

The function upper is not a word of the natural dictionary, and the list came back as [ "X", 1 ]. It ran anyway! The record already knows this escape and has routed its repair. Until the repair lands, "the natural layer is a closed language" is true of its words and not of its lists, and this book will say so.

And the Hausa pack does not yet read the letter ɗ, which standard Hausa spelling uses. The pack stores it in an encoding that does not carry it yet. When I probed it on 8 October 2026 on the snapshot before this commit, a sentence written with the letter was not read, and the pack did not report it. The Hausa in this chapter is written without the hook, the way the pack reads it today. The record holds no reading of the pack's sentences by a Hausa speaker. The foreign-language sentences printed in this chapter come from the library's narration and guards, or are composed from its vocabulary. No native speaker has read them as far as the record shows.

These are the limits; the next section opens six doors on them.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerYou keep writing code. What you declare is a closed grammar, and the court judges your sentence and an AI agent's by the same rules.
The analystYour domain's words become a data pack, and the system understands them or refuses them with the reason.
The designerThe refusals are part of the language: what is off the list is refused in strict mode, so it never needs a warning.
The decision-makerAn AI model held to a declared grammar answers in the right shape. It can still answer a falsehood in the right shape, and the record prints that limit with the result.
The educatorA sentence in Hausa, French or Arabic runs and says back what it understood, so a learner reads the machine's reading of their own words.
The agentYou may speak only the declared language. Strict mode is your posture, and your draft is, by the vision's rule (designed), a proposal the court judges.

9. Exercise

Declare, with StzOutputSchemaQ, a record of three fields from a domain you know: a loan request, for instance, with an amount inside a band, a currency from a closed list, and a purpose in free text. Before you run anything, write three answers an AI model might give: one the court must accept, one it must refuse because of its shape, and one it will accept although it is false. Under each, write your prediction as a promise.

Run it. The third answer is the lesson of this chapter. Write down, in one sentence, who in your domain must judge it, since the grammar cannot.

I left this one in your hands. Section 7 says that a list written inside brackets is still handed to the host, and section 4 says why a language must refuse any form that reaches host code. Run the section 7 block with one change, a different host function inside the brackets:

Haro
? @@( Naturally("Create a list with [ lower('X'), 1 ] and remove its duplicates").Result() )

not run: an exercise, written for you to run

Look at what the library does with the function, and say in one sentence what a closed natural layer would have done instead. When you have, you will know why "the natural layer is a closed language" is true of its words and not yet of its lists.

Chapter 12 is A language, declared. Its principle: declaring a language is as easy as declaring a variable.

Part III · Chapter 12

A language, declared

Draft · not yet read by the author

Run on 2026-10-14 22:25 UTC+01:00 inside the library at commit 93d7a39bd: 8 of 8 blocks kept their promise.

The blocks were run by the runtime of the former host language, version 1.27; Haro does not run the library yet. The engine binaries were built in a checkout of this commit, newest built 2026-10-05 20:27 UTC+01:00; 1 engine change(s) committed after that build are not in them.

In this chapter I take one declaration of a restaurant's order and give it to three readers: a person, an AI model and the court. I let the same declaration produce a grammar, and I show where the grammar and the court agree and where they part. Then I leave the library for the forge. It is the machinery that turns a language's declaration alone into its court and its grammar, and I say what it has forged and what it has not. I decided that Haro is the language of languages, and I refused an open escape form. The principle is one rule of Haro: declaring a language is as easy as declaring a variable.

1. The concept, as the field holds it

Two families of tools let you declare a language in the field. The first is the language workbench and the parser generator: JetBrains MPS, Xtext, Spoofax, and Racket's #lang give you the means to define a language with its grammar, its editor and its checks. The estate's own field study of August 2026 says why they did not win. They depended on an ecosystem, and Racket's languages live and die inside Racket.

The second is the internal DSL: a library whose calls read like sentences, while the file can still hold any host code. The same study has the sentence I keep: closedness is the product, and an internal DSL that cannot refuse arbitrary host code is an API wearing a language's costume. Its control group is the closed languages that won: SQL, regex, Make, HTML and CSS, HCL, GraphQL, Markdown, CUE.

For the grammar a model must obey, the record names one tool: the grammar sampler of a well-known local inference library, which the library's machine follows for its element encoding and its algorithm. Nothing of it is vendored. It is general knowledge, not a study of the record, that model vendors offer structured-output modes that take a JSON schema, and that open libraries turn a schema or a regular expression into a mask on the model's tokens.

Chapter 11 told what a closed language is, and what was lost when the field left it open. I take that as read. This chapter says what is new: what produces a closed language.

2. The first principle

Declaring a language is as easy as declaring a variable.

It is the heading of one rule of Haro, ruled on 1 October 2026, and the kernel of the vision says the same: the era makes declaring a language as easy as declaring a variable. The other half of the chapter has its sentence, from the alphabet's totality doctrine, ratified on 27 September: malformedness dies at the sampler, falsehood dies at the court, and non-termination is unexpressible.

And the one I must carry beside every win, from the library's contract for structured output: structure kills malformedness, and not falsehood.

3. The Softanza form

Take a declaration of what a restaurant's order must look like. It has three fields: a dish from a closed menu, a quantity between 1 and 12, and an optional note. One text is read by three readers. A person reads a description. A model reads a clause for its prompt. And the court reads the same text and judges an answer. What does it answer to a dish called pizza and forty portions? Run it:

Haro
oO = StzOutputSchemaQ([
	[ :field = "dish",     :type = :oneof,  :choices = [ "margherita", "tiramisu" ] ],
	[ :field = "quantity", :type = :number, :must = [ [ ">=", 1 ], [ "<=", 12 ] ] ],
	[ :field = "note",     :type = :string, :optional = 1 ]
])
? oO.Describe()
#--> schema 'output' -- 3 field(s)
#      dish : oneof (margherita | tiramisu) [required]
#      quantity : number [required], must be at least '1', must be at most '12'
#      note : string [optional]
? oO.PromptClause()
#--> Answer with ONLY this structure, one field per line, nothing before it and nothing after it:
#
#    dish: <one of: margherita | tiramisu>
#    quantity: <number>
#    note: <text>
aV = oO.Verify([ :dish = "pizza", :quantity = 40 ])
? aV[:ok]
#--> 0
? aV[:findings][1][:message]
#--> field 'dish' is a closed enumeration (margherita | tiramisu) and the model answered 'pizza'.
? aV[:findings][2][:message]
#--> field 'quantity' must be at most '12', and the model answered '40'.

ran: printed what this block promises

The court answers in the declaration's words: field 'dish' is a closed enumeration (margherita | tiramisu) and the model answered 'pizza'. Now the same declaration produces a grammar. The court and the grammar are born of one text, and they agree on the shape. They part ways on a value. Forty portions has the right shape: which of the two lets it through, and does the library say what the grammar dropped? Run it:

Haro
cG = oO.ToGBNF()
cGood  = "dish: margherita" + nl + "quantity: 2" + nl + "note: no basil" + nl
cBand  = "dish: margherita" + nl + "quantity: 40" + nl + "note: no basil" + nl
cShape = "dish: margherita" + nl + "quantity: many" + nl + "note: no basil" + nl
? StzGrammarAccepts(cG, cGood)
#--> 1
? oO.Accepts(cGood)
#--> 1
? StzGrammarAccepts(cG, cBand)
#--> 1
? oO.Accepts(cBand)
#--> 0
? StzGrammarAccepts(cG, cShape)
#--> 0
? oO.Accepts(cShape)
#--> 0
? len(StzFind("lessequal", oO.UnenforcedByGrammar())) > 0
#--> 1

ran: printed what this block promises

The second pair is the point of the chapter: the grammar answers 1 and the court answers 0! I do not print the list of what the grammar dropped: its text carries, in one place, the court's former name, and that name belongs to the history in Appendix H. I test that the list names the limit of the range.

An AI model is not asked to be careful. The sampler asks the grammar at every candidate token whether it could continue. So a word that is not on the menu is not refused after it is said. Can it begin at all?

Haro
? StzGrammarCouldContinue(cG, "dish: t")
#--> 1
? StzGrammarCouldContinue(cG, "dish: p")
#--> 0
? StzGrammarCouldContinue(cG, "dish: margherita" + nl + "quantity: 2")
#--> 1
? StzGrammarCouldContinue(cG, "dish: margherita" + nl + "quantity: <")
#--> 0

ran: printed what this block promises

It cannot: dish: p answers 0. The last line is a failure the measurement of section 5 found in a small model: the placeholder <number> echoed where a number belongs. And a token is not a byte. A piece may be valid as a prefix and invalid as a completion, and the machine is fed the whole piece. What does it answer to yesterday, which begins like yes?

Haro
cY = 'root ::= "yes" "\n"'
? StzGrammarCouldContinue(cY, "y")
#--> 1
? StzGrammarCouldContinue(cY, "ye")
#--> 1
? StzGrammarCouldContinue(cY, "yesterday")
#--> 0

ran: printed what this block promises

The pieces y and ye answer 1, and yesterday answers 0!

What the machine will not hold, it refuses by name. A closed language refuses what it cannot carry, and never approximates. A left-recursive rule is refused by a code, and so is a rule referred to and never defined. A nested structure is refused by the grammar. Does the court still read it?

Haro
? left(StzGrammarRefusal('root ::= tail' + nl + 'tail ::= tail "x" | "x"'), 7)
#--> GBNF-M7
? left(StzGrammarRefusal('root ::= greeting'), 7)
#--> GBNF-M4
? StzGrammarRefusal(cG) = ""
#--> 1
oNest = StzOutputSchemaQ([
	[ :field = "title",  :type = :string ],
	[ :field = "author", :type = :structure, :fields = [ [ :field = "name", :type = :string ] ] ]
])
? oNest.IsExpressibleAsGrammar()
#--> 0
try
	oNest.ToGBNF()
catch
	? len(StzFind("GBNF-F5", cCatchError)) > 0
done
#--> 1
? oNest.ParseOutput('{ "title":"T", "author":{"name":"Ada"} }')[:ok]
#--> 1

ran: printed what this block promises

The text of the nested-structure refusal carries the court's former name too, so I print only the codes. The last line is the point: the court reads what the grammar refuses to write.

The declaration language is itself closed. A typo in the law is refused when the law is declared. The library's contract says why. A key such as :requird = 0 would leave a field required without a word, and that is the class of typo a court must not tolerate in its own law. What does the court answer to one?

Haro
try
	StzOutputSchemaQ([ [ :field = "x", :type = :string, :requird = 0 ] ])
catch
	? cCatchError
done
#--> stzOutputSchema: unknown key ':requird' in field #1 (use :field, :name, :type, :required, :optional, :choices, :oneof, :of, :fields, :must, :note, :description).

ran: printed what this block promises

The typo was refused at once, and the message lists the keys that are allowed!

And a host function is not a word of the closed language of conditions. There are two ways to say a condition, the closed language and the door of a function. A square root is a word of the engine's expression language, and a sine is not. What does the textual form answer to the sine, and what does the function form, which runs host code?

Haro
o = new stzList([ 4, 7, 10, 3, 8 ])
? @@( o.FindW('{ sqrt(@item) < 3 }') )
#--> [ 1, 2, 4, 5 ]
? @@( o.FindW('{ sin(@item) < 2 }') )
#--> [ ]
? @@( o.FindWF( func x { return sin(x) < 2 } ) )
#--> [ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 ]

ran: printed what this block promises

What I saw, and the narration does not say: the refusal is silent and whole. The textual form printed [ ] and the function form printed [ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 ]: nothing from the one, everything from the other. A condition with the true left branch and a sine on the right printed [ ]. A condition that calls a function of mine never called it. A syntax error also printed [ ]. The language is closed, and it refuses without a word. Chapter 11's natural layer says why it refuses, and this one does not.

The forge, outside the library

A language declared once should give its court, its mouth, its voice and its readers. That is the forge, and it is where the study of this book meets its own limit: the forge is not in the library.

I will say what the record holds, and what I observed on 8 October 2026 on the older runtime, the oracle. The record is a charter and a spike in another repository, in pure core code that runs on the oracle. The forge reads a declaration and writes two files, a court program and a grammar. The spike's rungs, between 1 and 4 October 2026, forged courts and grammars for the machine language of the estate and for a fleet language declared over it. They did the same for the expression language and for four more letters of the alphabet, the vision's family of declared languages, each known by a letter. Each was judged against the pre-existing language's own cases. Those cases were unadapted for the expression language (W) and for Z, re-expressed for F and A, and, for Q, the older language's own answers, captured. In order: 117 of 120 for the machine language, the three left being the fleet file's kinds. Then 32 of 32 for the fleet language, 29 of 29 for W, 16 of 16 for Z, 25 of 25 for Q, 26 of 26 for F and 35 of 35 for A. This is chapter 3's method, declare then govern, applied to the forge itself.

I ran the forge on a small language I wrote for this book, a table's order in the words of the dining room. It is an example, written for the book and run once, outside the library:

DEFINE LANGUAGE order AS ( VERSION "0.2", GRAMMAR "0.2", COURT "none", EXTENSION ".order" )
  RATIONALE "A table's order, in the words of the dining room"
DEFINE MENU dishes AS ( WORDS [margherita, tiramisu, chianti],
  MESSAGE "the kitchen cooks margherita, tiramisu or chianti" ) RATIONALE "The kitchen's closed menu"
DEFINE RANGE portions AS ( MIN 1, MAX 12,
  MESSAGE "{value} portions is not an order: one to twelve" ) RATIONALE "A table orders between one and twelve"
DEFINE DECLARATION line AS ( VERB "ORDER", SEATS [dish: dishes, quantity: portions, note: text?] )
  RATIONALE "One line of an order: what, how many, and a word for the kitchen"
DEFINE REFUSAL unknown_verb AS ( MESSAGE "The dining room speaks only of orders." )
  RATIONALE "The closure speaks when an alien verb arrives"

The forge printed that it had forged one kind and one refusal, in a fraction of a second of wall time, and wrote a court of about 2.6 kilobytes. What did that court answer to a dish off the menu, to forty portions and to an alien verb? It refused all three, in the declaration's own words:

DISH pizza          ->  order (line 2): the kitchen cooks margherita, tiramisu or chianti, not 'pizza'
QUANTITY 40         ->  order (line 3): 40 portions is not an order: one to twelve
DROP TABLE orders   ->  order (line 1): Unknown verb 'DROP': The dining room speaks only of orders.

The refusals are the declaration's own words, written beside the grammar. Even DROP TABLE orders was refused in the dining room's words! This is the whole of the evidence for the order language: it ran once, outside the library, and it is not a declaration of the record.

Three more observations, each a limit.

The meta-court refuses the escape. The declaration of the language of declarations lists the operators and operands it may use. A declaration that listed eval among its operators, in a fixture pinned on 29 August 2026, was refused: eval is not in the closed operator menu, an escape hatch is unexpressible, not forbidden. A host call among the operands was refused in the same way.

The forge's grammar holds shape only. A menu seat comes out as a general identifier, so the forged grammar lets pizza through. The library's own schema compiler, in the blocks above, closes the same menu into an alternation. On the estate's machine language, the forged grammar accepts a dangling reference that the court refuses. The record names a difference between mouth and court, the part that a context-free grammar cannot say: duplicate names, dangling references. I found no record that states the menu gap as a gap.

The vision has not caught up. The vision's text, dated between 27 September and 5 October 2026, says the forge has not forged. The principles file, dated 1 October 2026, says that the forge does not exist. The same repository built the spike the same day and forged for several languages. So the true sentence has two sides. The forge has forged courts and grammars for several languages, outside the library, and it has not forged the full list the principle promises. And the vision's text has not been updated. In the book's stage words, the forge is built outside the library and designed for the library, and chapter 11's limit says the same.

The parts of a declared language

The charter lists what the forge produces from a declaration, its parts, and I give each a stage word:

partwhat it isstage
the textthe declaration, plain and closed, with a rationale required on every declarationbuilt outside; the library's analogue is the schema declaration
the courtthe judge generated for the language, speaking in the declaration's own wordsbuilt outside; the library's analogue is Verify and Accepts
the mouththe grammar for a constrained AI modelbuilt in the library for schemas; built outside for declared languages, shape only
the promptthe instruction an AI model reads, tuned by measurementbuilt in the library; not known for declared languages
the person's readinga description for a humanbuilt in the library (Describe)
the voicethe language narrating a run, a sentence, a refusal; never stored and never parsed backbuilt outside; the library's analogue is Understood()
the tonguesa human language as a data filebuilt outside for two tongues; built in the library for five packs (chapter 11)
the projectionsthe world rendered to an application, a server, a page, a devicedesigned
the facetsa second syntax of Harodesigned; chapter 16 tells it

The word facet has two meanings in this book, and I define the one of this part here. A facet is a second syntax of Haro, for a programmer of another language: another spelling of the one grammar, and never a runtime. It is the last row of the table, and chapter 16 tells it. The other sense is a tab of the environment's ribbon, one phase of a life, which is chapter 26's.

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I decided that Haro is the language of languages. The charter's header quotes me, from 1 October 2026: Haro is a language of languages, in which the crafters define a language for their domain and program in it, or let their AI agents. The charter records a reversal: its first decision, as the general-purpose floor under the family of declared languages, was reversed. The rest of that ratification was my "go with your recommendations" on seven decisions, and those are rulings by delegation.

I decided to declare, and not to write. The act of the kernel: declare a language. It was extraction and not invention: the first languages were declared after they already ran and had consumers.

I refused an open escape form. No clause, operator or operand denotes host code, calls, evaluation or input and output. Unexpressible, not forbidden. Two fixtures pin the refusal, and I re-ran them.

I refused logic in the declaring surface. The declaration declares and does not compute. The alphabet is deliberately not Turing-complete, and that is its power and not its poverty. This is my view.

I refused natural language as the declaring surface. Natural language asks, and it never declares. A draft may be proposed, and the court decides, and the human ratifies.

I refused one text for declaring and for computing. Programmability and closure never occupy the same surface. Computing code reaches a declared world only through the doors the forge generates, and chapter 16 is about the door.

I refused to let the grammar half retire the court. The contract says the court does not retire when constrained decoding lands. And what the grammar cannot express it refuses, and never flattens or approximates.

I refused a second facet as a second meaning. A facet spells the graph; it never gives it Python's or JavaScript's meaning. That is a session's memo, which proposes and rules nothing, and its question of how many facets before the announcement is mine, and unanswered in the record.

Next is the court, and the guards that stand behind it.

5. The court

structuredoutput_narrated proves that a declaration is judged when declared, with an unknown type, an unknown key and an empty menu refused. It proves that two wire shapes are read and nothing is guessed, that there is no partial credit, that nesting works, and that a retry fits in one budget. In its tenth scene, it proves that a lie is let through on purpose. schema_grammar_narrated proves that the declaration compiles to a grammar, and that a closed enumeration becomes a closed alternation. It proves that optional and list arity are handled, that the unenforced constraints are listed by field and operator, and that a nested structure is refused with a named code. constrained_decoding_narrated proves that the machine walks a grammar byte by byte, that a prefix is not a whole, and that yesterday is refused. It proves that the placeholder the model wrote cannot be reached, that refusals are named, that structure is not falsehood, and that a grammar on a streaming session is refused. Its two scenes that need a generative model say so. 483_w_and_wf_forms_in_conditional_code proves that the two forms of a condition give the same positions. It does not assert the closed language's refusal, and no guard does.

No guard in the library tests a forge, since there is none. The forge's guard is outside: the spike passes twenty-three stages in 367.5 seconds on 4 October 2026, by its own file. I did not run it. And the meta-court's own first run was twenty-eight of twenty-eight on 29 August 2026. The book's guard reader resolves only guards in the library's test tree, so these cannot be named in the front matter.

The first attempt is valid in two cases of ten when checked afterwards, and in ten of ten when constrained. That figure is a number in a comment of these guards. It cannot be re-taken here: the live scenes need a generative model file, and the snapshot holds only a checksum file in its folder for models. Chapter 11 carries the figure, and I point to it.

Read from the library's test tree at commit 93d7a39bd on 2026-10-14 22:28 UTC+01:00. The figure is the number of assertions the guard holds, counted in its file; the site shows each one run.

  • structuredoutput_narrated73 assertionsbase/test/neural/structuredoutput_narrated.ring
  • schema_grammar_narrated28 assertionsbase/test/neural/schema_grammar_narrated.ring
  • constrained_decoding_narrated50 assertionsbase/test/neural/constrained_decoding_narrated.ring
  • 483_w_and_wf_forms_in_conditional_code2 assertionsbase/test/list/483_w_and_wf_forms_in_conditional_code.ring
  • calc_column_engine_narrated14 assertionsbase/test/table/calc_column_engine_narrated.ring

6. The field, and where it leads

The workbenches lead on tooling. The field study says it itself: they remain superior on the axes the design deliberately abandons, projectional tooling, editor integration and depth of macros. And the bet that those axes are the wrong ones is named as a bet.

Generated code makes undisciplined language-making cheap too, and that is why the court is the core and not an accessory.

Constrained decoding: the field built it first, and the reference implementation is another library's. What the record adds is the pairing: a grammar and a court from one declaration, and the list of what the grammar dropped.

A grammar over-approximates a court. Duplicate names, dangling references and the coherence of a menu are not context-free. I observed it both ways above: a band the grammar cannot carry, and a reference it cannot carry.

The code a forge emits must be read by someone. The family style that every declared language inherits has a success test, that learning the second language should take an evening, because it is the first language with different verbs. It is a design requirement and not a measurement. No learner has been timed in the record I read.

The limit comes next, at the edge of a second closed language.

7. The limit

  • builtin the library: a declaration judged when it is declared; a court and a grammar from the one declaration, with the list of what the grammar dropped; a grammar machine that walks bytes and refuses by name; a description for a person and a prompt for an AI model from the same text. Outside the library: a forge that turns a declaration into a court and a grammar, run on the estate's own languages
  • designedthe forge inside the library; its full list of products from one declaration (printer, knowledge graph, natural door, narration, runtime, one static binary); the projections of a language to an application
  • absentthe forge's grammar for a menu word; a guard that asserts the refusal of a host function in a condition; the figure two of ten against ten of ten, which needs a model file the snapshot does not hold

The library has two closed formula languages, and they behave differently at the edge. A reader who takes the closed condition language of chapter 11 and of the condition above to cover every formula will be wrong at the table. The calculated column of a table falls back, by its own header, to the classic evaluation path when the engine cannot compile a formula. Does the word sin that the condition refused run here?

Haro
o1 = new stzTableAggregator([
	[ :A, [ 0, 1, 4 ] ],
	[ :B, [ 2, 4, 20 ] ]
])
o1.AddCalculatedCol(:SINE, 'sin(@(:A))')
? @@( o1.Col(:SINE) )
#--> [ 0, 0.84, -0.76 ]

ran: printed what this block promises

The sine the condition refused, the table computed, and it printed [ 0, 0.84, -0.76 ]! I also saw, and do not show, a second thing. On another probe table, with A as 1, 3 and 10 and B as 2, 4 and 20, I wrote a formula @(:A) + HostBonus(@(:B)). The function of mine inside it multiplies by a thousand. The formula printed [ 2001, 4003, 20010 ]: a user-defined host function ran from inside a formula string. And a formula that names a function that does not exist raised the host's own error. So the second closed language is open at its edge. No guard asserts either behaviour.

What is built: in the library, a declaration judged when declared; a court and a grammar from it; the list of what the grammar dropped. A grammar machine that says it is constrained; a prompt and a description from the same text. The build counts 151 assertions in three narrated guards. Two closed little languages of conditions, with limits. The natural layer's tongues as data.

What is built, but outside the library: a forge from a declaration to a court and a grammar, in the Haro charter's repository.

What is designed: the forge producing from a declaration alone the parser, court, printer, grammar, knowledge graph, query grammar, natural door, narration, runtime and one static binary. By my reading of the charter, the spike has shown the court, the grammar, a runtime that walks the declaration, a query grammar, a narration and the court of the natural letter. I did not find shown a printer for declared sentences, a knowledge graph forged from a declaration, or the one static binary per language. The library having a forge: nothing in it declares or forges a language. A grammar for every declared language shipping in the library: promised in the kernel, not shipped. And the projections: the world rendered to an application, a server, a page, a device.

What is absent: the forge's grammar for a menu word, which I saw above holds shape only, and the figure of two of ten against ten of ten, re-taken. And any record that the forge runs on the Haro runtime. At the time of the vision's writing the language did not exist; the charter's runs are on the older runtime and on the oracle.

The six doors follow, from the programmer to the agent.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerYou declare the shape in a few lines and get its court, its grammar and its prompt from them. What you do not get is a way to run a host function from the declaration: the language has no word for it. The table's formula language of section 7 is another language, and open at its edge.
The analystThe declaration is plain text in the domain's words, and the court answers in those words.
The designerThe refusal is declared beside the grammar, in the domain's voice, and is not authored per runtime. A designer chooses what a closed menu says when it is broken.
The decision-makerOne declaration produces the mouth and the court, and the forge itself publishes where they disagree. The forge is outside the library today. Do not buy it as shipped.
The educatorThe reader can predict, byte by byte, what the sampler will allow, and learns that a grammar kills malformedness and not falsehood.
The agentYou speak only the grammar you were handed. A sentence you draft is a proposal that the court judges. Your mouth is shape, and your falsehoods are the court's and a person's.

9. Exercise

Write, by hand, a grammar for one line of a lunch order: dish: then one of two dishes of your choice, then a newline. Before you run anything, write your predictions as promises:

Haro
cG = 'root ::= ...'     # your grammar here
? StzGrammarAccepts(cG, "dish: <your first dish>" + nl)
#--> ?
? StzGrammarAccepts(cG, "dish: <a dish not on your menu>" + nl)
#--> ?
? StzGrammarCouldContinue(cG, "dish: <the first letters of your first dish>")
#--> ?
? StzGrammarAccepts(cG, "dish: <the first letters of your first dish>")
#--> ?
? StzGrammarRefusal(cG) = ""
#--> ?

not run: an exercise, written for you to run

Then add a number to the line, quantity: and digits, and write a sixth prediction: does your grammar accept quantity: 4000? Run it. The lesson is the third, the fourth and the sixth. The machine already knows that a prefix could continue and is not yet a sentence, and it cannot know that the number is too large. Write down, in one sentence, who in your restaurant must refuse forty portions, since the grammar cannot.

I left this one in your hands. Section 3 ends its run of conditions on a refusal without a word, and section 4 says why computing stays off the declaring surface. Take the two lines that put the same question to the list in the two forms, and change one thing: write another number in place of the 2, the same in both lines. I print nothing under them.

Haro
o = new stzList([ 4, 7, 10, 3, 8 ])
? @@( o.FindW('{ sin(@item) < 2 }') )
? @@( o.FindWF( func x { return sin(x) < 2 } ) )

not run: an exercise, written for you to run

Run them for several numbers. Look for a number at which the two forms print the same thing, and say whether the printout alone tells you which of the two refused and which answered. When you have, you will know what it costs that a closed language refuses without a word.

The next chapter turns to the natural sentence, in two directions and under one discipline. A sentence runs because every word of it is in a dictionary the library owns, and what the library does not know, it refuses, with the reason.

Part III · Chapter 13

Natural, and executable: two directions, one discipline

Draft · not yet read by the author

Run on 2026-10-14 22:25 UTC+01:00 inside the library at commit 93d7a39bd: 17 of 17 blocks kept their promise.

The blocks were run by the runtime of the former host language, version 1.27; Haro does not run the library yet. The engine binaries were built in a checkout of this commit, newest built 2026-10-05 20:27 UTC+01:00; 1 engine change(s) committed after that build are not in them.

In this chapter I run the two directions of natural language in the library: the chain, where you are the parser, and the sentence, where the library is. I print the refusals on both sides, five language packs as data and a sixth added at runtime, and the count of what each pack can say. I say what I refused, the markers on reference and the ungrammatical chain among them, and where the dictionary's own court fails at this commit. The principle is one sentence. A sentence runs because every word of it is in a dictionary the library owns, and what the library does not know, it refuses, with the reason.

1. The concept, as the field holds it

In the field's common language, "programming in natural language" means one thing: asking an AI model for code, or asking it to do the task, in a prompt. The tools are chat assistants and code completers, in wide use since about 2021. What the sentence runs on is the model's guess. The same sentence may give different code on different days, the model needs a network or a local runtime, and a person reads the result to know what was understood. Chapter 11 said it, and I point back.

Older practices exist, and the record names them. Inform 7, a language whose programs are English sentences, compiled whole, with a world model and a way to say it across sentences. AppleScript, English-like and hard to write, because its naturalness was on the surface and not in a semantic model. Controlled natural languages, whose strongest device, the library's own comment says, is showing what can be said next. A session's reading of 30 August 2026 is that Inform 7 is a whole-text compiler with referential context, and not a command dispatcher. The dates are general knowledge, not a study of the record.

None of them is what the record claims. The claim is the opposite of prompting: a sentence executes because every word of it is in a closed lexicon, defined as data, mapped to a verb the library documents. Anything else is refused with the reason. And it has two directions, which the library's design review tabulates. In the first, the machine is the parser. In the second, the human is.

2. The first principle

A sentence runs because every word of it is in a dictionary the library owns. What the library does not know, it refuses, with the reason.

My study of the record, and the lede of the site's page of 8 October 2026, say it. For the second direction, the design review's thesis: in near-natural language, the human is the parser. And the older motto, which chapter 5 carries: what you think is what you write.

3. The Softanza form

I start with the second direction, because it is the older.

The human is the parser

A near-natural chain is a sentence in which every link is a real call. The sentence is "the word haro is a lowercase Latin word with a length of 4 letters and only 2 vowels". When it is false, what does the chain say? Run it:

Haro
? TheWordQ("haro").IsAQ([ :Lowercase, :Latin, :Word ]).WithQ().ALengthQ().OfQ(4).UnitQ(:Letters).AndQ().OnlyQ(2).VowelNB()
#--> TRUE
? TheWordQ("haro").IsAQ([ :Lowercase, :Latin, :Word ]).WithQ().ALengthQ().OfQ(4).UnitQ(:Letters).AndQ().OnlyQ(1).VowelNB()
#--> FALSE
? Why()
#--> no: expected exactly 1, found 2

ran: printed what this block promises

The chain answers no: expected exactly 1, found 2. Degree words are devices, and the reason is kept. The block reads it with the console's Why(); the chain also keeps its own, WhyCheckFailed(), which I do not call here:

Haro
? Q("AnnIE").AtLeast(2).VowelNB()
#--> TRUE
? Q("AnnIE").AtMost(2).VowelNB()
#--> FALSE
? Why()
#--> no: expected atmost 2, found 3

ran: printed what this block promises

The chain refuses what its subject cannot do. It speaks the same lexicon as the machine's direction: a French word works inside a chain. And a misspelled word is refused with the nearest word. This is "one lexicon, two directions" in three lines:

Haro
try
	Q(5).VowelNB()
catch
	? cCatchError
done
#--> NNL: a stznumber cannot count 'numberofvowels' -- and neither can the chain subject.
? Q("haro").IsAQ(:String).IfSo("majuscule").Content()
#--> HARO
try
	Q("haro").IsAQ(:String).IfSo("uppercse")
catch
	? cCatchError
done
#--> NNL: this stzstring does not understand 'uppercse'. Did you mean 'uppercase'?

ran: printed what this block promises

A chain branches on its own truth, and an ordinal is a word:

Haro
? Q("haro").IsAQ(:String).IfSo(:Uppercase).Otherwise(:Reverse).Content()
#--> HARO
? Q("hello").IsAQ(:Number).IfSo(:Reverse).Otherwise(:Uppercase).Content()
#--> HELLO
? Q("hello brave world").TheNth(2, :Words)
#--> brave

ran: printed what this block promises

Questions work the same way. A force word, the question's first word (What, HowMany and Is in the block below), opens a frame, one word and one method. A tag question ends in "or not". What does the session keep when one answers yes and the other no? It keeps every answer and folds them, like a narration:

Haro
? @@( WhatQ().TheQ().VowelsQ().OfQ("AnnIE").Is() )
#--> [ "A", "I", "E" ]
? HowManyQ().WordsQ().Of("hello brave world")
#--> 3
ClearAnswers()
? IsQ().TheQ().LengthQ().OfQ("Haro").TheSameAsQ().TheQ().LengthQ().OfQ("Ruby").OrNot()
#--> 1
? Why()
#--> yes: 4 is the same as 4
? IsQ().TheQ().LengthQ().OfQ("Haro").TheSameAsQ().TheQ().LengthQ().OfQ("softanza").OrNot()
#--> 0
? Why()
#--> no: 4 is not the same as 8
? @@( AnswersSoFar() )
#--> [ 1, 0 ]
? AllYesSoFar()
#--> FALSE
? AnyYesSoFar()
#--> TRUE

ran: printed what this block promises

The session kept [ 1, 0 ] and folded it: all yes is FALSE, any yes is TRUE.

The machine is the parser

Now the other direction. The sentence is a string, and the library reads it. The same verdict can come from a narration of questions and from a chain of truth. How sure is the chain of truth, and why? Run it:

Haro
oT = Naturally("Create a string with 'haro' Is it lowercase ? Does it contain 'r' ?")
? @@( oT.Answers() )
#--> [ 1, 1 ]
? oT.AllYes()
#--> TRUE
? oT.Understood()
#--> create a string with haro -> ask: is lowercase -> ask: contains
? TruthOf("haro").IsA(:Lowercase).AndIsA(:Latin).AndContaining("r").Holds()
#--> TRUE
? Why()
#--> yes: "haro" is lowercase and is latin and containing "r"
? Certainty()
#--> 1
? Evidentially()
#--> certainly

ran: printed what this block promises

It answers certainly, and says why: yes: "haro" is lowercase and is latin and containing "r".

The whole paragraph is compiled into code before anything runs, and the code is readable. It is the library's own account of why the layer exists:

Haro
o1 = Naturally("Create a string with 'test.data' Replace '.' with '_' Uppercase it")
? o1.Result()
#--> TEST_DATA
? o1.Code()
#--> oStr = StzStringQ("test.data")
#    oStr.Replace(".", "_")
#    oStr.Uppercase()
#    @result = oStr.Content()

ran: printed what this block promises

Does the same meaning in Hausa land on the same code? Hausa is written here without the hooked letter, as the pack reads it today, for a reason that chapter 11 gives. Run it, and each program says back what it understood, in its own words:

Haro
oE = Naturally("Make a string with 'hello niger' inside Spacify it and uppercase it")
oH = NaturallyIn("hausa", "Yi rubutu da dauke 'hello niger' a ciki Raba shi kuma maida shi")
? oE.Code() = oH.Code()
#--> TRUE
? oH.Understood()
#--> yi rubutu dauke hello niger -> raba -> maida
? oE.Understood()
#--> create a string with hello niger -> spacify -> uppercase

ran: printed what this block promises

The comparison answers TRUE: one code for two languages!

The sentence-dictionary is not the only vocabulary. Where does a word go that it does not hold? It is looked up in the library's own vocabulary, here the documentation tags of the uppercase verb. A value in quotes is data, and never a verb. An unknown word in a value position stays a literal:

Haro
? Naturally("Create a string with 'softanza' Capitals it").Result()
#--> SOFTANZA
? Naturally("Create a string with 'capitals' Uppercase it").Result()
#--> CAPITALS
? Naturally("Create a string with 'a-sep-b' Replace sep with '_'").Result()
#--> a-_-b

ran: printed what this block promises

The third line is also a limit: it printed a-_-b. The word sep was in no dictionary, and was used as the text to replace. A word it does not know is a literal.

Five languages as data. The dictionary is keyed by meaning, and each language's word lands on one id. Do a French, an Arabic and a Turkish word land on the same one? Run it:

Haro
? StzResolveSemanticInLang("fr", "doublons")
#--> METHOD_REMOVEDUPLICATES
? StzResolveSemanticInLang("ar", "تكرارات")
#--> METHOD_REMOVEDUPLICATES
? StzResolveSemanticInLang("tr", "tekrarları")
#--> METHOD_REMOVEDUPLICATES
? StzResolveSemantic("removeduplicates")
#--> METHOD_REMOVEDUPLICATES

ran: printed what this block promises

The languages follow their own grammar, and they are not word-for-word translations. Turkish puts the verb last, with the parameters before it. Arabic, with its vowel marks and a doubled letter, is stripped by the pack; the suffix on the verb is the masculine "it" for a text. French elides:

Haro
? NaturallyIn("tr", "'a.b' ile bir metin oluştur '.' yerine '_' koy").Result()
#--> a_b
? NaturallyIn("tr", "'haro' ile bir metin oluştur ve tersine çevir").Result()
#--> orah
? NaturallyIn("ar", "أنشئ نصا بـ 'haro' ثم اقلبه").Result()
#--> orah
? NaturallyIn("ar", "أنشئ نصًا بـ 'haro' ثمّ اقلِبْه").Result()
#--> orah
? NaturallyIn("ar", "أنشئ نصا بـ 'haro' ثم اقلبه").Understood()
#--> أنشئ سلسلة بـ haro -> اعكس
? NaturallyIn("fr", "Crée une chaine avec 'haro' et mets la à l'envers").Result()
#--> orah

ran: printed what this block promises

Three languages, three grammars, one answer: orah. Arabic says back what it understood, in its own words: أنشئ سلسلة بـ haro -> اعكس.

No native reader has read these sentences. They are modelled on the guard's, with 'haro' in place of the guard's own test word, and the Turkish string reversal is the book's variant of the guard's list reversal. I do not know that a speaker has read them. The record holds no reading by a speaker of the Arabic, Turkish, French or Swahili sentences, as it holds none for the Hausa of chapter 11. They are printed as sentences modelled on the library's own, unread.

Can a language be a block of data? Here is Swahili, added at runtime, by the guard's own words:

Haro
StzAddNaturalLanguage([
	:code = "sw",
	:name = "swahili",
	:script = "latin",
	:ignored_words = [ "na", "ya", "kwa", "hii" ],
	:semantic_mappings = [
		[:natural = "unda",   :semantic = "CREATE_OBJECT"],
		[:natural = "orodha", :semantic = "OBJECT_LIST"],
		[:natural = "na",     :semantic = "VALUE_INDICATOR"],
		[:natural = "panga",  :semantic = "METHOD_SORT"]
	],
	:phrases = [
		[:semantic = "METHOD_REMOVEDUPLICATES", :words = "ondoa nakala, futa nakala"]
	]
])
? StzHasLanguagePack("sw")
#--> TRUE
osw = NaturallyIn("sw", "Unda orodha na [ 9, 4, 9 ] ondoa nakala")
? @@( osw.Result() )
#--> [ 9, 4 ]
? osw.Understood()
#--> unda orodha na [ 9, 4, 9 ] -> ondoa nakala

ran: printed what this block promises

Four mappings, one phrase, and the sixth language answers [ 9, 4 ]!

Natural code is data too. A document's fenced blocks run, and a template is filled:

Haro
cDoc = "This tutorial explains deduplication." + nl +
	"#<" + nl +
	"Create a list with [ 3, 1, 3 ] and remove its duplicates" + nl +
	"#>" + nl +
	"The end."
? len( StzNaturalBlocks(cDoc) )
#--> 1
? @@( NaturallyFromDoc(cDoc)[1].Result() )
#--> [ 3, 1 ]
cT = "Create a list with {#1} and remove its duplicates"
? @@( NaturallyWith(cT, [ [ 5, 3, 5 ] ]).Result() )
#--> [ 5, 3 ]
? @@( NaturallyWith(cT, [ [ 9, 9, 4 ] ]).Result() )
#--> [ 9, 4 ]

ran: printed what this block promises

What the packs can say. How much does each pack say? The library has a function for it, and no guard prints its figures. I count against twenty-five reference meanings, which are the structural ones and every method and modifier any shipped pack names. They are not the thousands of verbs the library grew:

Haro
for cLang in [ "en", "ha", "fr", "ar", "tr" ]
	aC = StzPackCoverage(cLang)
	? cLang + " " + aC[:covered] + " of " + aC[:total]
next
#--> en 23 of 25
#    ha 9 of 25
#    fr 25 of 25
#    ar 16 of 25
#    tr 10 of 25
? StzHasNeuralModel()
#--> FALSE

ran: printed what this block promises

The Hausa pack speaks nine of twenty-five meanings: ha 9 of 25! And no model is loaded. The layer has an optional rescue by embedding, when nothing lexical was found and a model is loaded. At this commit none is, and none is needed. So I say "no model is loaded", and not "never touches a model".

From the 2020 diagram to the three eras

The library names three eras, in a design document of 10 July 2026. The first is near-natural language, the first paradigm. The second is natural programming: lower the language toward code, with free text, and one object per block. The third, of 2026, is one lexicon shared by execution and documentation, multilingual packs with morphology, and Understood(). I call the third the shared lexicon. The vision's own heading for it uses a word this book does not use.

Here are the dates, as the record gives them. My strategic diagram carries the years 2020 to 2025, shared on 13 September 2026; its Narrations band reads "executable natural language". The deck of 2022 was exported on 20 September 2022, and its slide 2 says to express thinking in an executable natural language. The library's repository begins on 12 March 2022, and its history cannot date 2020 or 2021. The near-natural files and the engine at its present path were first committed between 16 and 19 September 2025. On 30 October 2025 languages became configuration. On 2 November 2025 string input replaced brace capture. On 9 July 2026 the lexicon was unified from the documentation tags. On 10 July 2026 the two design documents were written, and the audit of fifteen canonical examples found that four ran, and two of those answered correctly. The site's flagship page is of 8 October 2026. The git dates come from the library's own repository, which the snapshot lacks; I checked them there on 9 October 2026, and the commits cited are ancestors of the pin.

So the earliest slide the record dates is the founding slide of the 2022 deck, exported on 20 September 2022. The year 2020 is the first year of my strategic diagram, which was shared on 13 September 2026; the record holds no slide of 2020.

Now the decision, and what I refused.

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I built it without an AI model, as a dictionary. The design says everything in the natural folder attacks one wall: the semantic gap between a human intention and its execution. The thesis of near-natural language, in that review: zero NLP, zero ML, native speed, full determinism, and the programmer in control. The natural vision's closing observation is that the layer delivered a fourth promise the old documents never dared to make: accountability.

I decided on two directions, one discipline. The review's table has five rows. Who parses: a machine with a lexicon, or the human. Ambiguity: refused loudly, or impossible by construction. Vocabulary: bounded by packs, or unbounded. Understanding: verified by the machine, or by a human reading. Audience: domain experts and AI agents, or programmers. Both end at the same place: a deterministic sequence of semantic operations.

I refused markers on reference. On 10 July 2026 I rejected the family of suffixes that marked a reference. The cipher was inverted by its own inventor from memory, it duplicated meanings, and language itself never marks reference this way. More than two hundred and sixty methods were removed. Chapter 11 tells it in two sentences.

I refused the ungrammatical chain. The chain is the sentence, and an ungrammatical chain that runs is a bug. I hold this as a view, not a result. The doctrine is held by reading aloud, not by a machine, and I show the proof below.

I refused negation as a prefix. Negation lives in negative forms, in antonym comparators and in the tag closer OrNot(). The tag question above is that ruling running.

I refused silent tolerance. The old typo tolerance was replaced by explaining everything: the refusal with the nearest word, above.

I refused global context. Two chains interleaved contaminated each other, and the fix put the context on the chain. The process-wide Why() remains as a convenience for the console and the tests. The globals survive as fallback shims: a legacy method outside the natural layer that builds a new object still falls back to them.

I refused the markup language. Annotations that handed the machine what it could not infer governed by making the human annotate. The system governs by dialogue. Two seeds were kept as thin doors, and they are the document and the template above.

I refused a command interpreter for narratives, and brace capture. In my own words in the article: it is designed for commands, not narratives. And one object per block. The string form replaced the brace form, because natural code became a first-class data type, storable, versionable and searchable. The rule since relaxed: a program may name objects and switch between them.

I refused governance inside the natural layer. I ruled that scope out of the library on 12 July 2026, and the code was removed.

I refused natural language as a way to declare. It asks, and never declares.

The court comes next, and one guard in it fails.

5. The court

nnl_narrated proves the flagship sentence, the generated surface of nouns, the degree words, the conditional mood, the ordinal reference, the refusal that accounts for itself, the grammaticality doctrine, context on the chain, and the discourse tense. multilingual_pack_narrated proves packs as data, programs in French, Arabic and Turkish that run, verified affix stripping, a language added at runtime, and Understood() back in the program's language. question_narrated proves the question frames and that a frame with no aspect is refused. literate_templates_narrated, the documents and templates. truthchain_narrated and interrogative_narrated, the folded verdicts.

semantic_resolver_narrated is the guard that ought to protect the dictionary, and at this commit it fails. I ran it twice on 8 October 2026 and each time it stopped with an error: three assertions failed, and the run ended after the twenty-ninth. In that run the word "caps", which the guard asserts, resolved to a method for bounds, and "mirrored" resolved to nothing. The reason is the design's own: the vocabulary is read from the library's documentation tags, plus seventeen hand-written operations grown by reflection to about three thousand. So a documentation edit changes what a word means. The library refuses honestly in the second case: in that run Unresolved() named the word and UnderstoodAll() printed 0. The court of the dictionary has failed on the dictionary, and chapter 11, chapter 22 and chapter 2 name this guard.

I ran the other guards named above once each on 8 October 2026, and in that run they passed all their assertions; the book's own data holds only their counts. The assertion calls written in the seven guards named above sum to 269.

Read from the library's test tree at commit 93d7a39bd on 2026-10-14 22:28 UTC+01:00. The figure is the number of assertions the guard holds, counted in its file; the site shows each one run.

6. The field, and where it leads

The field leads in breadth of phrasing. An AI model accepts any phrasing in any language, and the dictionary accepts what the packs name. Measured above: the Hausa pack covers nine of twenty-five meanings, Turkish ten, Arabic sixteen, English twenty-three (the two it lacks, English reaches through the grown vocabulary), French twenty-five. And the sentence layer acts on three classes only: strings, lists and numbers. A customer's domain objects are not among them; the domain goes through the knowledge graph.

The field leads in whole-program semantics. Inform 7 compiles a whole world. Here a program is a sequence of operations on a live object.

The field leads in an editor. In my run, the suggestion function answered nine continuations for a half-written sentence, and the code credits the controlled-language field for the idea. There is no editor here that shows them as you type.

And there is a loss on the library's own side. Understood() prints verbs and not their arguments: the block of section 3 prints contains and not the 'r' it asked about. In my run, Replace printed as replace, and Add 3 to it printed as add while the result was 8. A reader who checks the machine's reading sees no 3. This qualifies chapter 11's claim that a person can check what the machine understood.

Where the win is, with the loss beside it: the same sentence gives the same answer, with a reason, in the user's language, and designed to run offline, which no guard measures. The loss is that the user's language must be in a pack, and a word outside is a literal or a refusal. The record says the winning case is regulated or sovereign work: an instruction that executes locally and can be audited to the word.

The next section says where the chapter stops.

7. The limit

  • builtboth directions: chains where the human is the parser, and sentences where the machine is; five language packs as data and a sixth added at runtime; refusals with reasons on both sides; question frames; a thin truth chain; natural code as data in documents and templates
  • designeda grammar that holds an AI model to the lexicon; a guard that no socket opens during a natural run; the plan emitted as a chain; the article examples pinned as fixtures
  • absentany machine that judges a chain's grammar; Ajami, Zarma and Fulfulde; a natural layer closed all the way down; a dictionary protected from the drift of the documentation it is read from; the old articles' promises, several of which do not run

An ungrammatical chain runs. The second chain below reads "which a length of 4", which is not English. Does anything judge it? Run both:

Several chains of the near-natural article do not run at this commit: InLowercase() raises for lack of an object; LettersNB, BeforeQ and TheirQ().FirstCharQ() are not defined; and the brace form Naturally() { ... } raises for too few parameters. The bridging article's chain with ReplaceLowercaseCharsQ is not defined either. I ran twelve chains of the near-natural article on 8 October 2026, and eight work. The machine said so, since UnderstoodAll() is false and the unresolved word is named (the block above shows both), but a reader has to ask.

What is built: both directions; five packs as data and a sixth at runtime; refusals with reasons on both sides; the question frames, the thin truth chain, the evidential register; natural code as data. The folder holds thirteen files and about twelve thousand lines in twelve classes, by wc and grep on 8 October 2026.

What is designed: the plan of a narration emitted as an executable chain, so that chains gain Understood() for free. A grammar emitted for the natural lexicon, so that an AI model may only produce sentences the layer executes: I searched the folder, and no grammar emitter touches it. A guard that fails if a socket opens during a natural run, which does not exist. A coverage figure per pack printed by a guard. And the articles' examples pinned as fixtures.

What is absent: Hausa in the Ajami script, Zarma and Fulfulde. A natural layer closed all the way down: a plain list in a natural sentence reaches host code, which chapter 11 prints, and a descriptor reaches host code, above. Any machine that judges a chain's grammar. The standard Hausa letter, which the pack stores broken. A dictionary protected from drift. The record also holds no account, and no date, of my plea to the project of the former host language that natural programming be made a first concern, nor a sentence of mine in that voice that the book can source. All it holds is a private memo of 30 August 2026, which gives my judgement of the language's shipped natural form. The memo is marked private, so the book does not quote it and sources no phrase of mine to it.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerWrite the chain as the sentence and read it aloud. The library refuses what its subject cannot do, and says why. You are the parser, so the sentence is only as grammatical as you are.
The analystA requirement can be a paragraph that runs, with a paraphrase that comes back. Today it acts on strings, lists and numbers, so the analyst's domain words go in a knowledge file (chapter 14), not here.
The designerA designer's tone is in the refusals: a message names the word and the nearest word. The record has no designer-specific evidence for this chapter, and I keep the line short.
The decision-makerAsk any "natural language" claim what it does with a word it does not know. Here it reports it, refuses it in strict mode, or takes it as a literal, and says which. It is designed to run offline with no key. The no-network claim is not yet measured.
The educatorA learner writes in Hausa, French, Arabic or Turkish, and the program says back what it understood in the same language. The Hausa pack speaks nine of twenty-five meanings, and no speaker of those languages has read this page's sentences, as far as the record shows.
The agentSpeak the lexicon. Use strict mode and an allow-list (chapter 11). Expect refusal with a reason. Your sentence is a proposal. A grammar that would hold you to the lexicon is designed and not built.
