6. The field, and where it leads

My study of the record counted the constituent units of messaging, eighteen in all, and what is missing. Its sentence is that the word for a messaging app appears in no code file and no design document of the library, and USSD in none. I re-measured it at this commit and confirmed it. There is no hit in the code or the design of base, core or max. The matches in the rest of the snapshot are word-list and test data files, and USSD has none in text.

The frameworks lead in understanding and in connectors. Chapter 18 states Softanza's side from the code: the conversation asks one slot at a time, over a graph the user must first have declared. It does not understand an open reply.

The field leads in channel coverage and in delivery truth, receipts and provider-approved templates. The SMS port says it itself: a sink proves what you would have sent, not that a carrier would accept it, and the live adapter is infrastructure-gated. No live client for SMS ships.

The voice plan: a declaration is portable, and a voice is not. A browser's voice has no buffer, so the loop closes on the native tier only. This machine can speak English and cannot hear it.

What the field has in cloud dictation and in trained recognisers for many languages, the record chose not to ship. Free dictation reached 66.7 per cent on the plane's own clean synthetic audio.

What the record claims instead: the dialogue is a rendering of a declared world judged by a court, deterministic by default. The medium is a port with a sandbox, so the conversation and its bill are rehearsed before an account exists.

The field leads in places, and the limit comes next, printed whole.

7. The limit

  • builtthe governed conversation with its question as data; the SMS port and its sandbox, with the bill per segment in two alphabets; a verifier for the body of an inbound message; five semantic values rendered as colour, earcon and phrase; a voice that speaks, and hears a closed grammar; a closed set of sentences a business agrees to say; a message of three fields between identities of one platform
  • designedthe commons service of messaging; conversational surfaces for a messaging app, SMS, USSD and voice, with a satisfiability matrix as a court; templates as a grammar
  • absenta messaging app, USSD or a telephone line, in any form; a conversational projection of a world; a channel, a session, a template, consent; the question in a language other than English; a voice for Hausa, Zarma or Fulfulde; the twenty-two verbs as a list the library holds; a reply with a space in it

My study of the record has two errors that this chapter's runs correct. The first: it says speech to text is missing. At this commit it exists, by decision, for commands and not for dictation. The second: it says no message exists. There is a message of three fields, between identities of one platform, and I show it:

Haro
oDb = new stzDatabase(":memory:")
oCom = StzPlatformQ("neighbourhood")
oCom.OpenCommonsOn(oDb)
oCom.PostMessage("customer", "kitchen", "one brik, no egg")
? @@(oCom.Inbox("kitchen"))
#--> [ [ "customer", "one brik, no egg" ] ]

ran: printed what this block promises

It is a sender, a recipient, a body and a time in a SQL table. It has no medium, no status and no parts. It is the message my study found absent, in its smallest form.

What is built: the governed conversation; the SMS port and its sandbox; a body-signature verifier with replay protection, wired to no messaging provider; the semantic layer of five values rendered as colour, earcon and phrase. Also built: the voice; a minimal message in the commons; a closed set of sentences with a refusal; and the world's declared intents and reaches.

What is designed: Provides(:Messaging) as a commons service of the constellation. One design file says so, in two lines: a diagram that lists messaging among the commons, and a sketch that writes Provides(:Messaging). The word Provides is in no code file of the application folder. The commons runtime as the operational counterpart of the declared provides and shares. Conversational surfaces for a messaging app, SMS, USSD, voice and web chat, the satisfiability matrix as a court, templates as a grammar, a channel in the platform profile: these are proposals of my study of the record, written by a session, and not the library's design. A spoken analysis and a spoken transport: demos and compositions, and not a unit.

What is absent:

  • Ports for a messaging app, Telegram, USSD, and the telephone call: zero hits. A USSD session has no shape in the library.
  • A conversational projection of a world. The only projection is Generate, which knows three surfaces and refuses a fourth. No shell renders a question or a flow.
  • The messaging units: channel, session with a window or a timeout, template, consent. No unit of consent exists for messaging. The word consent appears in the snapshot for the microphone's boundary, in comments, and in two design documents in other senses.
  • The twenty-two verbs as a library list. stzApp holds five of them as five screen-intent methods, and the helper behind them does not check the word it is given. The other seventeen are in the constitution and not in the library. The bridge sentence is applied by hand today.
  • The question in a language other than English. AskIn is English, and the tutor shows the pattern in four languages. In my research run at this commit, NaturallyIn asked for Zarma raised the opaque "Unsupported object type!" and not "no pack for this language"; no block of this book records that call.
  • A voice for the languages that the product designs name, Zarma, Hausa and Fulfulde. None here; the library would refuse.
  • A reply with a space in it, from a phone. In my research run at this commit I ran ReplyIn("c", "grand couscous") and it raised, with an uninitialised variable. With a hyphen it was admitted. No block of this book records either result, as chapter 18 says of the same fault. This is chapter 18's known limit, and it is decisive here, because people type spaces in a text message. The conversation above works only because the replies are digits and one-word dishes.
  • Live adapters for SMS, for a messaging app and for a telephone line; delivery receipts; sender-ID rules.
  • Nothing in the record runs on a real phone as a conversation.

On(:whatsapp), On(:ussd), On(:voice) and the satisfiability matrix are what my study of the record proposed, and I do not present them as what I mean to build. I found no decision of mine to build them in the record, and the limit is the list above, in which none of them exists.

That is the limit, printed whole; the six doors follow.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerThe question comes back as data. You write the rendering and the reader for your medium in a dozen lines, and every reply goes through the same door whatever carried it.
The analystThe goal is the schema of the conversation. The transcript says which message produced which fact. The sandbox counts the bill before a provider exists.
The designerYour user keeps the phone they have: a text line with numbers, or a spoken phrase. The constitution's verbs are the grammar you render, and a verb the medium cannot render should be a red cell, and not a silent omission. That is designed and not built, since the matrix does not exist.
The decision-makerA conversation by SMS can be priced in a test: two Arabic dish names moved a 93-character question from one segment to two. The question to ask a vendor, what refuses a sentence your business did not approve, has an answer here: a closed set.
The educatorThe tutor already says the missing step as a question in four languages, in templates that carry no code. The record does not name a learner on a plain phone, and nothing serves one yet: there is no USSD and no messaging app.
The agentYou may propose a reply, and only a sentence of the closed set passes. An invented one is refused with its reason. And you cannot give a meaning to a phrase: the crafter declares it.

9. Exercise

Take a question your own world asks. The one-relation world of chapter 18's exercise will do. Before you run anything, write under each line the output you expect:

  1. the number of segments of your rendering of the question, with names in the Latin alphabet;
  2. its segments if one option is a word in Arabic script;
  3. what happens when the customer's reply is a digit that was not offered;
  4. what happens when the reply is "yes please".
Haro
? StzSmsSegments(YourRendering)[:segments]
#--> your prediction
? StzSmsSegments(YourRenderingWithOneArabicWord)[:segments]
#--> your prediction

not run: an exercise, written for you to run

Run it, with the sandbox and never a real send, so that the exercise touches nothing. If a promise breaks, do not change it: explain the output first.

I left this one in your hands. The fourth prediction is a defect I did not fix, and section 7 lists it in bold: a reply with a space in it, chapter 18's known limit. Take the block of section 3 that sends a reply to a question with no options on the table, change the reply "2" to a text with a space in it, and run it:

oKT = new stzKnowledgeGraph("trap")
oKT.Know("order1", "order")
oKT.AddConversationQ("c").SetGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireEach("order", "dish"))
oKT.AskIn("c")

The environment

Draft · not yet read by the author

Run on 2026-10-14 22:27 UTC+01:00 inside the library at commit 93d7a39bd: 10 of 10 blocks kept their promise.

The blocks were run by the runtime of the former host language, version 1.27; Haro does not run the library yet. The engine binaries were built in a checkout of this commit, newest built 2026-10-05 20:27 UTC+01:00; 1 engine change(s) committed after that build are not in them.

In this chapter I take the shape the field's environments have settled on, a toolbar, a sidebar, an editor and a status bar, and I set against it a pattern in five marks. I run the pieces the library has under those marks: a shell declared as text and judged, two projections, a ribbon in the order of a life, a rail that proposes, a status bar that tells the truth. I say what I decided, to carry both shells, and what I refused, among it a flag that turns the accessibility tree off. And I say where it stands: at this commit, an IDE of this family is absent, and the pieces beneath it run. The principle is one sentence: declare the interface once, and every shell is a projection of it that may add renderings, never verbs.

1. The concept, as the field holds it

The field's environments have settled on a shape. A toolbar and a menu at the top, a sidebar of files, an editor, a terminal below, and a status bar at the foot. Lately an assistant sits in a pane or a terminal beside the code, and the human approves its edits. I take that shape from general knowledge, and not from the record.

The record's own field studies, dated, are three. The notepad that ships with the former host language, measured on 12 August 2026 at thirty-three source files and about four thousand lines, seven dock widgets, a fifteen-key configuration and no language service. It exists, it ships in the box, and it works on the day you install it. The fast editors, in the ergonomics specification of March 2026, which sets for its own product: input to screen under sixteen milliseconds on any modern hardware, no exceptions. It wants minimal chrome, no status bar clutter, no toolbar forests. It asks for a dry run before a structural change, and for inspections that say why and offer a fix. And the status bar, as that specification wrote it: twenty-four pixels high, carrying only essential state, with five build states, one of which is unchecked, for a project where no build has run yet. The state of "not yet judged" has its own word. A bar that was green by default would be the field's usual lie.

Where the field is silent, the chapter answers. The field orders its toolbars by the tool's features, and not by the life of the thing being made. And it lets an assistant's proposal land as an edit, with the human's approval as a habit; that too is general knowledge.

2. The first principle

Declare the interface once. Every shell is a projection of it, and a projection may add renderings, never verbs.

The library's header for its authored interface says it: the file is the contract, and the native markup and the web page are its projections. My study of the record reads it as one declaration, two projections, proved to agree, resting on my ruling of 7 October 2026: carry both. The companion sentence is the interface constitution's, on the site: a new medium adds renderings, never verbs.

3. The Softanza form

First the stage, before the blocks. At this commit, an IDE of this family is absent. No class in the library is yet named for a ribbon, a rail, a spine or a status bar. My study of the record put it in a stage line proposed for the site: no IDE of this family ships today; one shell does, for the sound plane. The foundation that would make the next one a projection is specified and not yet built. I add one thing: the library generates one browser surface, the emulator's, and I show it below with a loss.

What the library has are the pieces under each of the pattern's five marks. The five are one shell, two projections, a facet ribbon ordered by the life of the solution, a rail that proposes and a status bar that tells the truth. They run, and I take them in order.

One shell, declared as text, judged by a court

The chrome is declared as text and judged before it is shown. The ribbon is generated from data, here a plain list; the facet as a library object is designed and not built. The four facet names are four of the five phases of the design corpus in the record: define, architect, build, govern, ship. I took four to keep the block short. Every declaration must carry its rationale, and a declaration without one is refused. Which element serves no verb? Run it:

Haro
aFacets = [ "Define", "Build", "Govern", "Ship" ]
cTabs = ""
cIds = ""
for cF in aFacets
	cId = "tab_" + lower(cF)
	cIds += cId + ", "
	cTabs += 'DEFINE TEXT ' + cId + ' ( CONTENT "' + cF + '", ROLE tab, SATISFIES select ) RATIONALE "A facet."' + nl
next
cShell = 'DEFINE PANEL shell ( SIZE [640, 360], DIRECTION column, FONT "app", SATISFIES locate, CHILDREN [ribbon, work, status] ) RATIONALE "One shell, three bands."' + nl +
	'DEFINE BOX ribbon ( HEIGHT 32, DIRECTION row, ROLE tablist, SATISFIES discover, CHILDREN [' + cIds + '] ) RATIONALE "Facets, in the order of a life."' + nl + cTabs +
	'DEFINE BOX work ( HEIGHT fill, DIRECTION row, CHILDREN [page, rail] ) RATIONALE "The workspace and its rail."' + nl +
	'DEFINE TEXT page ( CONTENT "the work", SATISFIES read ) RATIONALE "What is being made."' + nl +
	'DEFINE BOX rail ( WIDTH 160, ROLE group, SATISFIES preview, CHILDREN [advice] ) RATIONALE "What the court proposes."' + nl +
	'DEFINE TEXT advice ( CONTENT "no proposal", SATISFIES understand ) RATIONALE "The rail, empty."' + nl +
	'DEFINE BOX status ( HEIGHT 24, ROLE status, SATISFIES understand, CHILDREN [state] ) RATIONALE "The truth of the build."' + nl +
	'DEFINE TEXT state ( CONTENT "clean", SATISFIES understand ) RATIONALE "The court verdict."'
oShell = new stzUiDocument(cShell)
? oShell.IsClean()
#--> 1
? len(oShell.Declarations())
#--> 12
? @@( oShell.Orphans() )
#--> [ "work" ]

this block touches the system; the output shown was recorded on 2026-10-14 22:24 UTC+01:00

Orphans() answers [ "work" ], and IsClean() answers 1 over the 12 declarations.

The generating loop is the book's own, and the roles are from the closed list in the library: tablist, tab, group and status are on it.

The twenty-two verbs

Every element must trace to at least one verb, and a word that is not one of the twenty-two is found. There is a division of labour. The library records the claim, with SATISFIES, and finds the untraced elements, with Orphans(). It does not hold the list and does not refuse an unknown intent: the guard asserts that an intent nobody has defined is not an error. So the list below is typed from the constitution, which is in its own repository, and the book holds it. Does the court refuse an intent that is not on the list? Run it:

Haro
cShell = StzReplace(cShell, "DEFINE BOX work ( HEIGHT fill,", "DEFINE BOX work ( SATISFIES focus, HEIGHT fill,")
oShell = new stzUiDocument(cShell)
? @@( oShell.Orphans() )
#--> [ ]
aVerbs = [ "discover", "understand", "locate", "focus", "filter", "compare", "read", "scan", "scroll", "zoom", "select", "highlight", "preview", "mark", "act", "confirm", "cancel", "undo", "pause", "resume", "retry", "exit" ]
? len(aVerbs)
#--> 22
aStrangers = []
for cIntent in oShell.SatisfiedIntents()
	if not StzContains(aVerbs, cIntent)
		aStrangers + cIntent
	ok
next
? @@( aStrangers )
#--> [ ]
oOdd = new stzUiDocument(StzReplace(cShell, "SATISFIES preview", "SATISFIES transfer_funds"))
? oOdd.IsClean()
#--> 1
aStrangers = []
for cIntent in oOdd.SatisfiedIntents()
	if not StzContains(aVerbs, cIntent)
		aStrangers + cIntent
	ok
next
? @@( aStrangers )
#--> [ "transfer_funds" ]

ran: printed what this block promises

With SATISFIES focus on work, Orphans() answers [ ], and so does the loop over the book's list. Asked about transfer_funds, IsClean() answers 1! The loop over the book's list answers [ "transfer_funds" ].

work was a pure layout box, and the court counts containers too. Whether a container should be exempt from the verbs is the constitution's to say, and not the library's. The families, from the constitution: orienting, attention, information, selection, action, and continuity. And the interpretation I give: the library finds the stranger, and a list the library does not hold cannot refuse it. Chapter 25 said that the bridge sentence is applied by hand today. I tell the removal as the refusal at the centre of this chapter, in section 4: the library does not own the verbs, the constitution does. The library's own design text still says twenty-four; it is not the list. The twenty-two are printed in the block above, typed from the constitution as Appendix C prints them.

Two projections

The same text yields the native markup and the web page. Every declared element is in both, and the two spell a property differently exactly where the profile records a divergence. How many names are in both? Count them:

Haro
cRml = oShell.ToRml()
cHtml = oShell.ToHtml()
nBoth = 0
for cName in oShell.Names()
	if StzContains(cRml, 'id="' + cName + '"') and StzContains(cHtml, 'id="' + cName + '"')
		nBoth++
	ok
next
? nBoth
#--> 11
? len(oShell.Names()) - 1
#--> 11
? StzContains(cRml, "--rmlui-direction")
#--> 1
? StzContains(cHtml, "--rmlui-direction")
#--> 0

ran: printed what this block promises

Eleven elements and not twelve: the panel is the page itself, and not a div. The last two lines show where the two differ. The native markup holds --rmlui-direction (1), and the web page does not (0). The native tier lays out through the engine's layout library, vendored, and draws through the graphics plane. I did not open a window.

The browser shell

The browser shell is a page that the language serves, on the loopback. One request, one process, no network beyond 127.0.0.1. A second reactor plays the client, so it is offline by construction. The handler reads a global, because lambdas of the host language do not capture locals. Where does the page live? Ask the server:

Haro
$cShellPage = cHtml
oSrv = new stzAppServer()
oSrv.Get_("/", func oReq, oResp { oResp.Html($cShellPage) })
oSrv.Start(0, "127.0.0.1")
oClient = new stzReactor()
cCRLF = char(13) + char(10)
nJob = oClient.SubmitTcp("127.0.0.1", oSrv.Port(), "GET / HTTP/1.1" + cCRLF + "Host: local" + cCRLF + "Connection: close" + cCRLF + cCRLF)
? oSrv.ServeOne(3000)
#--> 1
cAnswer = oClient.AwaitTcp(nJob, 5000)
? StzContains(cAnswer, "200 OK")
#--> 1
? StzContains(cAnswer, 'id="status"')
#--> 1
? oSrv.Host()
#--> 127.0.0.1
oSrv.Stop()

ran: printed what this block promises

Host() answers 127.0.0.1. The cost of this shape is named in the record. A locally bound port is a surface and must be treated as one. In the charter's words, the design intent has been measured for a sound studio and not for an IDE. The library's backend already refuses to leave the loopback unauthenticated, at bind time; the bare server above does not check. What does the backend do with 0.0.0.0? Try it:

Haro
oT = new stzAppTopology("shell")
oT.AddDataset("notes", [ [ "first" ] ])
oT.SetDatasetColumns("notes", [ "text" ])
oBackend = new stzAppBackend("shell", oT)
bRaised = FALSE
try
	oBackend.StartOn("0.0.0.0", 0)
catch
	bRaised = TRUE
done
? bRaised
#--> 1
? oBackend.IsLive()
#--> 0

ran: printed what this block promises

It raises! bRaised answers 1, and IsLive() answers 0.

A status bar that tells the truth

A status cell is a function of the court's verdict, so it cannot say clean about a document the court refused. The function below is the book's own, over the library's IsClean() and its diagnostics. The status-cell class is not yet in the library, and the guard that a cell shows only what the court emitted is designed. The specification also names the state before any build, unchecked, and my function does not carry it. What does the cell say for a child declared nowhere, and for a role that is not on the list? Run it:

Haro
? ShellStatus(cShell)
#--> clean
? ShellStatus(StzReplace(cShell, "[page, rail]", "[page, ghost]"))
#--> refused: DANGLING_REFERENCE
? ShellStatus(StzReplace(cShell, "ROLE status", "ROLE sttus"))
#--> refused: UNKNOWN_ROLE

func ShellStatus(cText)
	oD = new stzUiDocument(cText)
	if oD.IsClean()
		return "clean"
	ok
	return "refused: " + oD.Diagnostics()[1][:code]

ran: printed what this block promises

The cell answers refused: DANGLING_REFERENCE and refused: UNKNOWN_ROLE, and clean only for the document the court kept.

And what a screen reader reads is emitted from the declaration. A region declared ROLE status is emitted into the accessibility tree with its rationale as its description, in reading order, and no flag turns the tree off. The layout needs a font file, and this block uses the system's. What does the tree say of the status region? Ask it:

Haro
oShell.UseFont("C:/Windows/Fonts/segoeui.ttf")
oP = oShell.ToPanel()
oT = new stzAccessibilityTree(oShell, oP)
? oT.NodeCount()
#--> 12
? oT.NodeOf("status")[:role]
#--> status
? oT.NodeOf("status")[:description]
#--> The truth of the build.
? @@( oT.ReadingOrder() )
#--> [ "window", "tablist", 'tab "Define"', 'tab "Build"', 'tab "Govern"', 'tab "Ship"', "group", 'label "the work"', "group", 'label "no proposal"', "status", 'label "clean"' ]

ran: printed what this block promises

The tree answers status, and for its description The truth of the build., the rationale word for word! The library's header says why: every toolkit gates accessibility behind a performance flag, which is where users silently get nothing. So here there is nothing to gate and nothing to forget to switch on. The same file says what a screen reader can operate, an AI agent can operate.

A rail that proposes

A rail is a view over what the world proposes. A pulse proposes and never relates. An act on the world clears a proposal, and the world's own status line counts from the same list the rail shows. What does the world propose, and what remains after one act? Run it:

Haro
oApp = StzAppQ("fieldvisits")
oApp.AddThingQ(:Client) { Has([ :name ]) }
oApp.AddThing(:Visit)
oApp.AddReactionQ(:Client).Unseen(90, :Days) { Propose(:Visit) }
oApp.AddInstance("amadou", :Client)
oApp.AddInstance("binta", :Client)
oApp.Live()
#--> [fieldvisits] is live -- 2 thing(s), 0 flow(s), 1 reaction(s), 0 goal(s); 2 proposal(s)
for aP in oApp.Proposals()
	? aP[1] + " " + aP[2] + " " + aP[3] + " " + aP[4]
next
#--> propose visit for amadou
#--> propose visit for binta
? oApp.Pulse()
#--> 0
? len(oApp.Proposals())
#--> 2
oApp.Relate("amadou", :visit, "visit-1")
oApp.Pulse()
for aP in oApp.Proposals()
	? aP[1] + " " + aP[2] + " " + aP[3] + " " + aP[4]
next
#--> propose visit for binta

ran: printed what this block promises

Live() prints its line, 2 proposal(s) at its end, and the judge compares what is printed. Before the act, Pulse() answers 0 and the rail still holds 2 proposals. After the act, one line remains: propose visit for binta. "2 thing(s)" counts the two things, Client and Visit, and not the instances. Chapter 20 owns the law beneath the rail, the proposal, the plan and the court.

And a screen is an intent. One place where the world speaks in verbs is its screens. Five methods exist: ToDiscover, ToUnderstand, ToFocus, ToSelect and ToAct. A sixth verb, ToCompare, does not exist. What answers when a screen asks for it? Run it:

Haro
oW = StzAppQ("fieldvisits")
oW.AddThingQ(:Client) { Has([ :name ]) }
oW.AddScreenQ(:Home)  { ToDiscover(:Client) }
oW.AddScreenQ(:File)  { ToUnderstand(:Client) }
oW.AddScreenQ(:Pick)  { ToSelect(:Client) }
oW.AddScreenQ(:Edit)  { ToAct(:Client) }
oW.Explain()
#--> WORLD fieldvisits   lives in: memory (not persisted)
#      BEING
#        client (name)
#      MET FROM WITHOUT
#        screen home: discover client
#        screen file: understand client
#        screen pick: select client
#        screen edit: act client
try
	oW.AddScreenQ(:Side) { ToCompare(:Client) }
catch
	? cCatchError
done
#--> Error (R3) : Calling Function without definition: tocompare

ran: printed what this block promises

The runtime answers, Error (R3) : Calling Function without definition: tocompare, and no court does: the intent word is stored as a string, and is not checked against any list.

That is what runs; now I say what I decided with it, and what I refused.

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I decided to carry both shells. On 7 October 2026 I was asked whether the foundation takes the native shell or the browser shell, and I answered: carry both. The consequence, as my study of the record states it, is that one chrome is declared once, and two shells project it.

I decided that the mechanics are the library's and the IDE is the product's. The library's design document: the paradigm mechanics are platform; the book, the brand, the IDE are product, and never leak. The foundation ships refinement as a library verb available to every program.

I removed the interaction engine. On 26 May 2026 my commit removed twenty-two modules invented by an AI agent that were not in the original Softanza, among them the interaction module. I read the date, the count and the list in the library's git history, commit b70f3ad91, and not in the pinned tree. Its design text, which says twenty-four verbs and laws enforced by the engine, is still in the tree. The constitution's list is twenty-two.

I refused to resolve intents inside the language of the panel. The panel declares no meanings: there is no :Danger and there never may be. The intent slot was left deliberately unresolved. Above, IsClean() answered 1 for transfer_funds: the panel judges no meaning.

I refused to author the markup, and I refused a script engine. The native markup is emitted, never authored; there is no script engine; flexbox only. That is the reason the chrome is a text file and not a class.

I refused a flag that turns the accessibility tree off. The tree block above printed status and The truth of the build. without a flag to set.

I admitted a lens that cannot capture. The estate's charter for its products: one truth, in files, and two lenses, which in the charter are its two products, the front-door IDE and the commercial studio, and not two shells. What the charter refused was frameworks that capture the work. A lens that cannot capture is admissible. The environment is a projection of plain text, and not a store.

A session removed a facet, and I restored it. The reference design records that the Connections facet was first-class in the prototype of June 2026, and was removed by an AI agent on circular reasoning. The removal cascaded into five documents. I reinstated it. The ribbon is mine to decide.

I accepted the browser shell with its cost, unmeasured. The charter of the front-door IDE chose a browser tab, built with the engine, with no install step, and named the loss.

The pattern was learned across six efforts in two years, one of them built, by my study's count of the record.

Next comes the court, with the guards behind these pieces and the ones that are missing.

5. The court

gui_stzui_narrated proves the closure of the panel court, a dangling reference, a duplicate, an orphan box, a missing panel, the mandatory rationale and a round trip. In scene 13 it proves the intent slot: SATISFIES, Orphans(), and that an intent nobody has defined is not an error. gui_profile_narrated proves that the profile is data, with three recorded divergences. It proves that one document has two projections and every declared element is in both, and that the fixture emits a self-checking page. The browser half of that guard is a procedure to reproduce. gui_tier_agreement_narrated proves that one display list rendered as vector and as pixels agrees to the pixel. It is not HTML against native. gui_accessibility_narrated proves the tree emitted from the declaration. 05_stzapp_live_narrated proves that a live world proposes and acting clears. emulator_narrated proves the generated surface of the emulator.

Three guards are to come: one that judges a shell against the twenty-two verbs, one that a status cell shows only what a court emitted, and one that says the two projections of a chrome agree in the browser. My study of the record lists them as absent, and the tree at this commit agrees.

The two-projections check can fail, and it did. The library's fixture is a page and not an assertion: it carries the web projection and the boxes the native layout produced. A script compares them and prints a verdict strip. A runner cannot judge it, so I read it by hand on 8 October 2026. On the chrome of the first block, eleven boxes with text in each region, the strip read "AGREE on every declared box of 11". Its note said that four boxes of automatic width differ, which is two shapers and not the profile. On the same three-band chrome with empty regions, the strip read "DISAGREE on 1 declared boxes of 3". The cause is in the web projection: an empty box is emitted as <div id="body"/>. An HTML parser reads that as an open tag, so the siblings that follow nest inside it. The native tier is unaffected. The fixture catches it! The library's guards do not yet, since their own showcase has no empty box: adding one is the next step. An empty workspace is the pattern's first state. So the strip tells the truth both ways, which is the chapter's fifth mark in one picture, and the web projection has a case to correct on exactly that state.

From the court I turn back to the field, and to where it leads.

6. The field, and where it leads

The fast editors set a bar that the record writes down as law for its own product: input to screen under sixteen milliseconds, a cold start under four hundred, no exceptions. The record has not yet measured it on either shell: a latency number is absent, and it is the next step.

A text change dirties the whole document. One bound value changed re-shapes every string, where a colour re-shapes one. The field's editors patch, and lead here today; that is general knowledge.

The browser costs what it costs: file access through the browser's model, a port to guard, and an unmeasured latency. The native shell costs a window system, and a GPU for the raster path.

The field has a language service, as general knowledge has it, and the record has a contract; the service is the next step. The world graph, stzWorldGraph, is the explorer's model: it reads the world file the service would emit, and it is loaded by no entry file: a block that calls it without a hand-written load fails.

The field's fast editor treats the status bar as clutter. The pattern keeps one and asks it to be true. That is a bet, and I hold it as a view, not a result; the record's own corpus argues the field's side in the same breath.

That leaves the limit.

7. The limit

  • builtthe interface as a text with a court that finds the element serving no verb; two projections of it, native and web, with a recorded table of divergences and a page that can say DISAGREE; the accessibility tree emitted from the declaration; a page the language serves on the loopback; a world that proposes and whose proposals clear when it is acted on; screens declared as intents; one generated browser surface
  • designedthe shell kit with two shells; the chrome as closed kinds (spine, ribbon, rail, status bar), none yet a class of the library; the facet as data; a rail bound to focus; status cells read from the courts, with a guard that a cell never shows a state the court did not emit
  • absentan IDE of this family; a list of the twenty-two verbs in the library and a refusal of an unknown verb; a guard that judges a shell against the verbs; an editor; a measured latency

The web projection does not yet carry roles, labels and intents. ToHtml emits an identifier, a style and the text only. The tree that carries roles is a separate artefact, as the block above shows, so a browser shell would infer from bare divs what the native shell emits. The plan itself says that the accessibility library it adopts has no web adapter.

The library's own mission control prints constants where the pattern asks for verdicts. The emulator generates a browser surface, a parts grid with status chips and fidelity badges, a device window and a console for each part. Its status words are constants of the device class and of the template, and they are not measured. Here a plan with one firmware part and one GPIO capability, and no pump anywhere. What does its page say? Build it and read it:

Haro

What is built: the interface as text with a court; four closed kinds, a closed list of nineteen roles, a closed field set, a mandatory rationale, a round trip to a fixpoint. Two projections, with a recorded table of three divergences and a page that can say DISAGREE. The accessibility tree, and a bridge that reaches a real screen reader's interface on Windows, read and not run by me. A declared value changes and the screen follows, with focus kept. A page hosted on the loopback, and a backend that refuses to leave the loopback unsigned. A world that proposes, screens declared as intents, one generated browser surface. And one binary shell, the sound plane's listening bench, in about seven hundred lines of Zig, which I read and did not build.

What is designed: the shell kit with two shells; the chrome as closed kinds named for the spine, ribbon, rail and status bar, none yet a class of the library. The facet as data, with its group, its place in the life, its artefact kinds, its court and its profile. The rail bound to focus, and the governance cells read from the courts, with a guard that a cell never shows a state the court did not emit.

What is absent: an IDE of this family. A list of the twenty-two verbs inside the library, and any refusal of an unknown verb: transfer_funds passes the court. A guard judging a shell against the verbs. An editor. A measured latency. I tell the pattern as designed, with the running pieces as evidence: the court of the chrome, the two projections, the accessibility tree, the page hosted on the loopback. No IDE of this family ships today.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerYou write the shell as text, and a court tells you the one box that serves no verb before anything is drawn. The same file is a native window and a page, and the library has a page that says when they disagree.
The analystThe ribbon is the order of your solution's life, and not of a tool's features. The status cell reads the court, and you can ask the world what it proposes before it is asked to act.
The designerYour interface has a constitution of twenty-two verbs and a closed grammar that adds renderings and never verbs. Every element must say which verb it serves, and the library already finds the ones that say none.
The decision-makerAsk of any environment three things. Does its status bar read a court? Does its assistant live in one panel and propose? And who judges that the two shells agree? Here the answers are: designed; designed, with the rail's law built beneath it in chapter 20; and a self-checking page, which caught the empty-box case when I read it by hand on 8 October 2026; no guard judges it yet.
The educatorThe exercise is a prediction: say what the court will answer before you run it. The status word that is a constant is a lesson in the difference between a label and a truth.
The agentThe shell is a text file that you can read and write, and the tree a screen reader reads is the tree you may read. Your proposals appear in a rail and commit nowhere.

The engine beneath: three layers, one engine, Haro

Draft · not yet read by the author

Run on 2026-10-14 22:27 UTC+01:00 inside the library at commit 93d7a39bd: 9 of 9 blocks kept their promise.

The blocks were run by the runtime of the former host language, version 1.27; Haro does not run the library yet. The engine binaries were built in a checkout of this commit, newest built 2026-10-05 20:27 UTC+01:00; 1 engine change(s) committed after that build are not in them.

In this chapter I load the three layers of the library, one entry file at a time, and count what each holds. I read the engine beneath them, its eighty-nine libraries and the functions it registers, and I let the court say whether it is optimised. I set down the decisions, that the future is Haro and that every feature is implemented once, in the engine, and I print the rows where a fast peer still leads. The principle stands over all of it: the surface is the promise, and the runtime is the part you measure, and never assert.

1. The concept, as the field holds it

A platform inside one codebase is drawn as a stack with one rule: an inner layer knows nothing of an outer one. The cleanest peer, as my study of the record puts it, is Rust's three crates for three depths of host, chosen by the target; Rust enforces the rule by its compiler, which is general knowledge of the field. Softanza holds it by entry files, and section 7 says what that costs.

The field's habit for an engine is a native library with a plain C interface, wrapped thinly by each language. SQLite is the common example, well established in the field: one C library, bindings in nearly every language. The record states the same design for its engine: language clients are thin bridges that add syntax and paradigms, and never computation.

And the field has done, repeatedly, a third thing: a language keeps its surface and its libraries and changes the machine beneath. The record's own example is a typed descendant of Lua. Another, well established in the field, is the alternative implementation of Python. Both teach the same thing the record teaches: the surface is the promise, and the runtime is the part you must measure.

The principle that follows is one sentence, and section 2 sets it down.

2. The first principle

Every feature is implemented once, in the engine. The surface is the promise, and the runtime is the part you measure, and never assert.

The first sentence is the engine architecture's design rule, in a session's document: every feature is implemented once, in the engine. Language clients are thin bridges that add syntax and paradigms, never computation. Chapter 4 told my ruling that follows from it: I refused computation in the faces. The second sentence is the brief of the runtime beneath: performance and portability, measured, never asserted.

And the definition that governs the engine's dependencies, which chapter 4 already states: sovereignty is nothing anyone else can withdraw. In the vision's words, it never meant every line ours.

3. The Softanza form

Three claims, and a block for each of what a block can prove. I tell you first what a block cannot prove, because it matters. The dependency rule of the layers, that no core file loads base and no base file loads max, needs a scan of about eight hundred and seventy load lines. Only a guard could carry that, and none exists. I did the scan with a script of my own, and section 7 gives its result.

A layer is the file you load

How many classes does each entry file load? Three entry files, three fresh processes. Each prints how many classes it holds, and whether stkList, stzList and stzListXT exist. The block spawns child processes, because this chapter's own process has already loaded the largest layer, and only a child can show the core alone:

Haro
cAsk = 'aC = ringvm_classesList()' + nl +
       '? "" + len(aC) + " " + (find(aC, "stklist", 1) > 0) + " " + (find(aC, "stzlist", 1) > 0) + " " + (find(aC, "stzlistxt", 1) > 0)' + nl
aEntries = [ "core/stkLib.ring", "stzLib.ring", "max/stxLib.ring" ]
for i = 1 to 3
    write("layer" + i + ".ring", 'load "../../../' + aEntries[i] + '"' + nl + cAsk)
    ? trim(systemcmd("ring layer" + i + ".ring"))
    remove("layer" + i + ".ring")
next
#--> 17 1 0 0
#--> 674 1 1 0
#--> 714 1 1 1

The contract says base builds on core, by inheritance or delegation. What do the classes say? ringvm_classesList() returns, for each class, its name, its identifier, and its parent:

#--> stzcorestring

#--> stzobject

#--> stzobject

func ParentOf(cClass)
    n = find(aClasses, lower(cClass), 1)
    if n = 0  return "(not loaded)" ok
    return aClasses[n][3]

The second line prints stzobject: stzString inherits stzObject, and not stkString! Core carries a parallel hierarchy, in which stkString inherits stzCoreString, the first line's stzcorestring. Max does build on base: stzListXT inherits stzList, the last line's stzlist. Exactly two base classes inherit a core class, stzSciNumber and stzPointer, and one delegates, in a line of stzPointer. They are two among the hundreds of base. The contract is not met, and it is not met in the way chapter 4 asked about. I print it as a debt.

The engine does the work. What does the host's upper make of the German sharp s, and what does the engine's case mapping make of it, its own table over a vendored library? A second vendored library stems words. These are two of the engine's nineteen vendored libraries, which section 4 counts:

The decisions come next, and the first of them is about that future.

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I decided that the future is Haro, and not the former language. My words of 7 October 2026, as my study of the record quotes them, the bracket mine: the future is Haro, not [the former language], and the site must be clear about it. Haro's face of the former language will be maintained only so that the code already written continues to work. What is not carried is that language's runtime and its governance. The first ruling, on 28 August, was that it is not carried forward at all; it was superseded two days after, as the vision's amendment says.

I decided that the rewrite is a rename. The code of my articles, the narrations, rewritten in the name of Haro, is the same as the former language's face. The charter measures the same: Haro's own stages run the same text, byte-identical on the new compiler and on the oracle.

I decided that Haro is the language of languages. The charter's header quotes my note of 1 October 2026. The charter was ratified that day, with my "go with your recommendations" on seven decisions. Its amendments of 4 October answer nineteen open questions of the record, and the version stays ratified until I have read its section 15.

I decided that the surface is kept. Its surface today is the one the compiler compiles. The library is its compatibility specification. Other surfaces are faces over one program graph: every syntax a face, so that an AI agent fluent in the former language, in Python or in JavaScript writes Haro. Of these only the first face exists. A Python-shaped face is a spelling, not Python.

I removed the old framework, with no fallback. Engine-only: no fallback, no feature flags, no Qt dependency. The status of 12 June 2026 says zero of them remain. I checked. No loaded file loads a Qt library. Two external extensions are loaded by name: a zip one, which base loads, and a cryptography one, in a folder that no entry file loads.

I directed that the language's own extensions be removed. My directive of 13 June 2026: ensure that no external extensions are required, and that engine alternatives replace them. The library still loads one of them, a zip extension, as the entry above says.

I put the engine in Zig, with no dependency on a library, as my study of the record reports my ask. It is qualified by the record's own definition of sovereignty: nineteen vendored libraries, each with a record.

I let everything go into base. My sentence, as my study of the record reports it: under the pressure of time, everything went into base, waiting for the right moment to refactor again. By my count below, base is ninety-three per cent of the lines.

I chose safe optimisation. Not the fastest mode, and not the unoptimised one. I chose it because a clean panic beats silent memory corruption.

I refused a headline that does not reproduce. The memo of 13 September 2026 says the claim to retire is that the runtime beats the fast peer, present tense, on x64. Chapter 22 told the refusal, and section 6 prints the rows.

I refused a percentage. The figure is mine, and it should not be printed without the guard that produces it. Chapters 31 and 33 say so.

I have no sentence on how a layer is chosen in Haro. My study of the record only proposes that, in Haro, layer selection should be a declaration the compiler honours. The charter has no text on core, base and max. Base inheriting core is the contract as designed, with the stage word designed. The code does not meet it today, as section 3 prints, and the book's account is what the code does: two implementations over one engine. And in Haro, a layer is chosen by the file you load, today. A declaration the compiler honours is my study's proposal, and is designed.

Section 5 reads what the court proves of all this, and what no guard proves.

5. The court

engine_is_optimised_narrated proves that the engine is compiled with optimisation: twenty sums over two million doubles under a tenth of a second, and the right answer. It proves that an index of 99 and an index of 0 are refused and the buffer unharmed, and that the vendored parser which the optimised mode once broke now answers. I ran it: six of the seven assertions in the file were reached, and six passed. engine_senses_narrated proves that the engine gives the process five senses: memory, its peak, system memory, processor time, and a bounded series. I ran it: thirty-six of thirty-six, and the run then stops with "STOPPED!" by design. wasm_narrated proves that the engine's entry for the browser exports its curated interface and that the build has a target for it. It builds a subset and asserts that it is smaller. I did not run it, because it calls a build of the toolchain. threat_model_narrated reads the threat model and checks that each guarantee row names a proof and that each guard file it names exists. Rows G11, the fuzz harnesses, and G25, the bill of materials with its digests, concern the engine.

What does not exist: no guard judges the layers. No file under the test folders loads a layer's entry file or reads the contract. There are 529 narrated guards in base, and none in core or in max. My study of the record says 517 in one place and 387 in another, and the site 501; I print only what the build reads. And no guard judges the engine's counts: the numbers the engine's command-line status prints are typed constants dated 16 June 2026.

6. The field, and where it leads

Speed. The runtime beneath against a fast scripting runtime of the field, on 13 September 2026. The method is the memo's own: six pairs of kernels written fresh, identical algorithm and sizes on both sides, each side in its fast idiom, checksums across languages asserted before any number. The minima are over three inner repeats and two process runs, the new compiler built for speed, the peer interpreter-only with no JIT, on Windows, x64. The peer leads every row:

The memo's words: the peer leads every row, fib and binsearch are near-ties, and nothing is worse than 2x. ARM is unmeasured. The win that the memo keeps: within 2x on every row, which no version of the former runtime ever was.

The headline is still alive in the repository's own notes. As I read on 9 October 2026, the brief of the runtime's own repository and its notes still say that the spike beats the peers on every row. The correction is carried in another repository of the estate and in the memo. In the runtime's own record it is carried only for its release-candidate configuration, in one section of the notes. The memo asked for it. The memo of 13 September 2026 withdraws the claim, and the six rows above are its rows, although the repository's notes still carry the old claim. I name no peer, and describe it as chapter 22 does: a fast scripting runtime of the field.

Memory. On the same day the note says: resident, running the library, this morning 733 megabytes, now 149, and the former runtime 139. A loss of ten to the former runtime, after a fall of 584. A win and a loss in one note.

Compatibility, on 5 October 2026. The wide suite of the library was run on a snapshot. The note records parity of assertions on every one the former runtime passes, that most programs agree on every stable line, and that nineteen rows differ in kind. The note does not say Windows in that entry, and the Linux pass is listed as the next step. These are a session's notes from a private branch, and no number of mine. I print them, dated 5 October 2026, with the stage word in development: 8,540 of 8,540 assertions at parity, 1,253 of 1,253 tests that bear assertions, and 3,425 of 5,112 programs identical on every stable line. Another 1,267 are identical but for the line that prints the elapsed time, and 19 rows differ in kind: 13 print more, 5 are refused or raise, one writes a stderr line. They are the note's counts; the note does not place the remaining programs, and I ran none of them.

The platform. Built and run on Windows today. A Linux build of eighty-five of the eighty-nine modules exists on a working branch; the site says it is in construction. A whole program with its engine in one file, with no dependency, is absent.

The engine against the field. The threat model's row for fuzzing says it itself: no scheduled or coverage-guided fuzzing, no continuous integration and unsigned commits, which I deferred for the development phase. The field's maintained native libraries have continuous fuzzing and signed releases. And chapter 22's loss, unchanged: no collation by locale, and no time zones.

Section 7 says where the layers and the engine stop.

7. The limit

  • builtthree layers chosen by the entry file you load, each including the one beneath and none above; the dependency rule held at the loads; an engine of eighty-nine libraries, in Zig, built in optimised safe mode, with the engine's own count of what it exposes; Haro as a ratified charter and a spike whose courts run on the new runtime and on the old one
  • designedthe base layer inheriting the core layer; the max layer as a built layer; a court that checks the layers against their contract; a layer chosen by a declaration the compiler honours; the other faces of Haro over one program graph; a loader for one domain of base; the standalone engine repository and its command line; the engine's polyglot bridge, which is chapter 16's
  • absenta lean core layer that runs its strings; a Linux or macOS engine in service; a measured pass of the library on the new runtime under Linux; a haro executable; Haro running the library; a single executable with no dependency; an engine test count that I may print

The lean layer does not run. What does a string of the core give back when I ask it for its content?

Haro
o = new stkString("abc")
? o.Content()
#--> Error (R3) : Calling Function without definition: stkenginestringfrom

ran: printed what this block promises

The runtime answers: Error (R3) : Calling Function without definition: stkenginestringfrom. The core string cannot give back abc! The core string class calls engine names that no engine library registers. In a process of the core alone, the engine's core library registers five hundred and thirty-four functions under the base names and none under the core names. That count is from my notes, and no block shows it. So stkString and stkChar find nothing. My study of the record files it as an open item of the core and the engine. stkList runs, which chapter 4 showed, and the load of seventeen classes in a tenth of a second is real.

The lean layer is not lean at the binary, for strings. By file size, on the build of 5 October 2026, the core string library is 22,355,968 bytes and the base one 22,362,624. The read-only data is 20.8 megabytes in both; I did not diagnose what it holds. The four core libraries total 24.1 megabytes of the eighty-nine libraries' 122.4. The core libraries for dates, files and locale differ from their base twins by under one per cent.

The dependency rule holds at the loads, with one exception at a call. I parsed every load of every non-test, non-archive file of core, base and max, 871 lines, and resolved each. Core loads, outside its own folder, only the engine face; base loads core and the engine; no file under base loads anything under max or future; max loads base. But FindMin, in the core's list of numbers, calls a function that is defined only in base. In a core-only process, FindMin([4,2,9]) answers 2, and FindMin("not a list") raises "Calling Function without definition". In a base process it raises the intended error. I found one instance by a search for base names in core, and I did not look for others.

On a case-sensitive disk the core entry file does not load. Its second line loads a file by a name in the wrong case. My scan finds twenty such loads in non-test files at this commit; the runtime's own record counted fifty-five with tests, on 8 October 2026. The book is built on Windows, which hides it.

The third layer is written and not wired. Its thirty-two classes are all in one folder, and no entry file loads them. The first of them works when loaded by hand. I ran it and do not show it, a string of eleven characters counted by it. I tried none of the other thirty-one. A library layer for them in the engine does not exist.

What is built: a layer is a folder, a prefix and an entry file. I counted on 9 October 2026 at this commit, by files with the extension, excluding test and archive folders. Core, 27 files and 6,366 lines; base, 984 files and 519,579; max, 115 and 31,292; and a folder of the future, 51 files and 6,356. Base is 93.2 per cent of the three layers' lines. The engine: eighty-nine libraries from the Zig sources, 401 source files, 179,985 lines, and 2,464 declared tests, which I did not run. The toolchain is Zig 0.15.2 by the build file's own comment. Nineteen vendored libraries, each with a record of component, version, source, licence and digest. The record's own gaps: an archive digest is recorded for nine of the nineteen, and three have no version.

What is designed: the base layer inheriting the core layer. The seven shared domains are implemented twice over the same engine. Max as a built layer. A loader for one domain of base. A court that checks the layers against their contract. The standalone engine repository and its command line, which the architecture lists as a phase. The engine's polyglot bridge, which is chapter 16's.

What is absent: a Linux and a macOS engine in service; a measured pass of the library on the new runtime under Linux; a single executable with no dependency; an engine test count that I may print.

Haro

I tell what is built, what is designed, and what is absent, as the record has it on 9 October 2026.

Built, as a charter, a family of grammars and a guard. The charter, version 0.2, ratified on 1 October 2026. A spike of nineteen steps, which the record calls rungs, between 1 and 4 October, each a grammar document with fixtures. Its guard reported a pass of the whole run on 5 October. Its courts are programs that run byte-identical on the new compiler and on the official former runtime. The new compiler also formats and dumps the library's files: of about six thousand, nearly all print the reference's bytes, and a few dozen are refused by both. A first slice of a graph of the code was built on 5 October.

What Haro is today, in one sentence the record supports: a ratified charter and a spike whose courts run on the new runtime and on the old one, over the surface the library is written in. There is no haro executable. The folder of binaries holds the compiler and two others. The forged courts load no library. Haro does not run the library. The vision of 27 September said that Haro does not exist and that the new runtime's Linux row is unmeasured. The first half is out of date, since a charter and a spike exist. The second half is still true of the wide suite on Linux.

Designed: the three altitudes, declaring, declared, and computing; the six letters of its alphabet, which the charter names, five of them forged whole in the spike; refinement as the write surface; other faces over one program graph. Those faces arrive as printers before they arrive as parsers, and never as semantics. The verbs haro forge, check, refine, run, project and narrate are a recommendation, and not a program.

The runtime beneath, as the record dates it. Its brief: a register machine and a compiler from the former language's source to its bytecode, running existing programs. About three hundred thousand lines of Softanza are its compatibility specification. Its public face: the main branch is public and untouched; the work lives on a branch pushed to a private remote only. Its last commit at my reading is of 8 October 2026, at 22:26. The stage word is mine, and it is "in development".

The six doors follow, one for each reader.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerYou choose your depth by the file you load, and you can prove it in three fresh processes. The lean layer does not run its strings today: reach for base. Read the engine's count the way the library sees it, and not the way a page types it.
The analystThree numbers for "how big is the engine", and three methods. Ask which one a vendor means. The core library is the size of the base one for strings.
The designerA layer is a decision about what you ship, and not about taste. At the binary, core and base have a library per domain and the third layer has none; the web subset, which chapters 4 and 24 show, is a subset and not a layer.
The decision-makerThe two questions of chapter 4, plus two. What runs it: version 1.27 today, with the replacement in development. What the replacement measures: within 2x of a fast peer on every row, by 1.04 to 1.88 times, which no version of the former runtime ever was, and ten megabytes of memory more than the old one. This is my view: a record that prints its loss is the only kind to trust.
The educatorTeach the dependency rule by making a learner load the core alone and predict, then count. Teach "measured, never asserted" with the memo of 13 September 2026.
The agentYou may count the engine's functions yourself. Do not repeat a count from a page, and do not write a loop over the list of classes directly. Tell the reader which layer a class lives in by its parent chain, and not by its prefix.

9. Exercise

Before you run anything, write three numbers: how many classes each entry file will load, and which of stkList, stzList and stzListXT each holds.

Haro
# core/stkLib.ring, stzLib.ring, max/stxLib.ring: write your three predictions here,
# then load each entry in its own process and count with ringvm_classesList().

not run: an exercise, written for you to run

Then choose any class of the library, predict its parent, and read it with the parent chain. Write the line your prediction got wrong. A learner who guesses that stzString inherits stkString is in good company: the contract says so, and the library does not. I do not say which of the 17, 674 or 714 is which.

I left this one in your hands. The count by prefix in section 3, [ 10, 693, 0 ], is correct, and it says nothing about layers. Write that count again so that it asks each class's parent chain, read with ParentOf, and not its first three letters, and look at what you get. Section 3 says what the prefix hides, and section 8, the agent's door, says why I refuse it. When your count answers, you will know why a class's layer is read from what it inherits, and not from what it is called.

The next chapter leaves the engine for a restaurant in Lyon, and for the one sentence the project there taught: deliver small, fast and useful, and let the foundations mature in parallel without ever blocking a delivery.
